## Statement

Let $(D,p)$ and $(D',p')$ be finite regular diagrams of nonempty oriented links related by a planar isotopy or one oriented Reidemeister move, with the marked point on an unchanged exterior arc and carried to the corresponding point. The normalized integral signed Khovanov complexes have explicit bigraded chain homotopy equivalences whose maps and inverse homotopies commute with the marked actions $X_p,X_{p'}$. Consequently the quotients $C(D)/\operatorname{im}X_p$ and $C(D')/\operatorname{im}X_{p'}$, with their reduced quantum degree $j-1$, are bigraded chain homotopy equivalent. The conclusion holds over $\mathbb F_2$ by reducing these same integral formulas. It permits arbitrary other link components and arbitrary exterior connectivity. This local statement does not assert a relative movie theorem or canonical identifications between different move sequences.

## Statement references

[[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]]

[[lem-khovanov-signed-local-cancellation-models]]

[[lem-khovanov-reidemeister-chain-homotopies]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The two diagrams, one unchanged exterior mark, and the actual signed cubes, with local crossings ordered first.

[F1] The integral algebra, gradings, cube edge signs, multiplication and comultiplication are specified by [[def-khovanov-frobenius-algebra-and-cube-of-resolutions]].

[F2] [[lem-khovanov-signed-local-cancellation-models]] supplies the explicit RII and RIII integral retractions for every fixed exterior resolution and proves they commute with exterior saddle differentials and every exterior marked dot, including when several local arcs lie on one global circle. Its proof gives the inverse crossing-order state factor $(-1)^{v_1v_2}$ and the two-sided inverse-pair retractions.

[F3] [[lem-khovanov-reidemeister-chain-homotopies]] supplies the normalized shifts, the integral positive and negative curl contractions, and the six RIII height variants obtained by stacking the explicit inverse pairs. Its unreduced clause is for arbitrary links; its reduced Statement is knot-specialized, so the arbitrary-based-link conclusion is proved below rather than imported.

[F4] A chain homotopy equivalence is specified by maps $i,p$ and homotopies with $pi$ and $ip$ homotopic to the corresponding identities ([[def-chain-homotopy-equivalence]]).

## Proof

1.1 The marked action commutes with every edge. For a merge this is $m(Xa,b)=Xm(a,b)=m(a,Xb)$; for a split it is $\Delta(Xa)=(X\otimes1)\Delta(a)=(1\otimes X)\Delta(a)$, checked directly on $a=1,X$. Edges disjoint from its circle commute as tensor maps. Therefore $\operatorname{im}X_p$ is a subcomplex for any number of link components. The quotient replaces exactly the marked circle factor by $M=\mathbb Z$, $X=0$, with surviving label $1$; its reduced degree is $j-1$. The reduced interval formulas are $m_M(1\otimes1)=1$, $m_M(X\otimes1)=0$, and $\Delta_M(1)=X\otimes1$. This calculation uses no connectedness of the original link. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For R1, put the small-circle factor first and write a tensor as $(a,b)=1\otimes a+X\otimes b$, with $x$ the dot on the continuing arc. The positive raw differential is $(a,b)\mapsto a+xb$. Set $i(v)=(-xv,v)$, $p(a,b)=b$, and $h(v)=(v,0)$ from degree one to degree zero. Then $pi=1$, $di=0$, and on degree zero $1-ip$ sends $(a,b)$ to $(a+xb,0)=hd(a,b)$; on degree one $dh=1$. For the negative raw differential $d(v)=(xv,v)$, put $i(v)=(v,0)$ into degree one, $p(a,b)=a-xb$, and $h(a,b)=b$ from degree one to degree zero. Here $pd=0$, $pi=1$, $hd=1$ on the source, and $dh(a,b)=(xb,b)=(1-ip)(a,b)$ on the target. These are the actual curl contractions, with the raw degrees and quantum shifts of [F3]. Every exterior marked action commutes with $x$ and these coordinate maps: if the mark is on the continuing global circle it acts on $a,b,v$ by $x$, and otherwise the maps are identities on its factor. Exterior saddle compatibility follows from the merge/split identities in step 1.1; the small circle is inside the move disk, so an exterior saddle never touches it. Thus the contractions apply to the whole signed exterior cube for an arbitrary based link. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 For RII and the model RIII use exactly [F2]'s tensor maps and contractions. Its exterior-resolution convention orders actual global circle factors and defines every saddle as multiplication or comultiplication according to actual merging or splitting; it explicitly covers several local arcs on one circle, and the marked interval module. Thus neither an unknotted exterior nor a one-component link is assumed. All coordinate changes, inverse unit pivots and their homotopies commute with $X_p$ by [F2]. The other crossing order is corrected by the scalar factor $(-1)^{v_1v_2}$, which also commutes with the marked action. The six strict RIII height orders follow from the model equivalence by stacking the explicit inverse-pair retractions of [F2], as proved in [F3]. These composites and their homotopies still commute with the marked action, since sums and compositions of intertwining maps do so. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For completeness, on local degree $r$ the total differential is $d_{\mathrm{loc}}+(-1)^r d_{\mathrm{ext}}$. A local degree-zero map commutes with this signed total differential. A local homotopy lowers $r$ by one, so the two exterior terms in $dh+hd$ cancel. Therefore the local homotopy equations in steps 2.1 and 2.2 are equations for the full cube, not just a fixed resolution. The raw shifts are exactly those of [F3]: a positive curl has survivor $\{1\}$, a negative curl $[-1]\{-2\}$, an inverse pair $[-1]\{-1\}$ and RIII none, in its convention $C[s]^i=C^{i+s}$, $M\{s\}_j=M_{j+s}$. The changes of the normalization $[n_-]\{2n_--n_+\}$ cancel them. Thus the resulting full maps and homotopies preserve normalized quantum degree. A planar isotopy relabels the actual resolution factors, carries the marked factor with it, and preserves the signed cube; a crossing-order interchange contributes only the scalar $(-1)^{v(a)v(b)}$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Every map and homotopy just constructed intertwines the two marked actions. It therefore takes the image of the first action into the image of the second and descends to the quotient. Each homotopy equation descends as the same integral equation. By [F4] the quotients are chain homotopy equivalent; subtracting the same one from their quantum degrees preserves the bidegrees. Tensoring these explicit identities with $\mathbb F_2$ proves the mod-two claim. All sums, label orderings, retractions and crossing permutations are finite. No assertion about a chosen component surviving a whole movie, or about relative endpoint movies of multiple cut components, enters this local proof. [F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. A bridge diagram is a smooth regular oriented planar link diagram with nondegenerate height-critical points, distinct heights for all critical points and crossings, and no height-critical crossing preimages. A bridge isotopy is a smooth family of bridge diagrams. A bridge-like rectangular diagram is nonempty and has vertical-over-horizontal crossings, distinct horizontal levels and distinct vertical abscissae; each horizontal segment is either a local maximum or minimum without crossings, or is height-monotone after smoothing and contains exactly one crossing. Smoothing means tilting each crossing-containing horizontal segment slightly in the direction of height travel and rounding corners in disjoint small neighborhoods, retaining all crossings and their decorations.

Every nonempty bridge diagram admits a bridge-like rectangular diagram whose smoothing is bridge isotopic to it. Any two bridge-like rectangular diagrams with bridge-isotopic smoothings give grids related by finitely many legal column commutations, after replacing their ordered levels and abscissae by consecutive grid coordinates. In particular this construction is independent, up to grid commutations, of every coordinate choice. The orientations determine the alternating $O,X$ markings by the row $O$-to-$X$ and column $X$-to-$O$ convention of the grid-diagram definition.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and the finite oriented bridge diagrams or bridge isotopy in the statement. A legal column commutation exchanges adjacent columns whose closed vertical intervals are disjoint or one is contained in the interior of the other.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] defines the rectangular grid, crossing and marking conventions.

## Proof

1.1 A nonempty compact closed component has a height maximum and minimum, so there are at least two special points and the grid number below is at least two. Cut each underpassing branch at each crossing, but do not cut the overpassing branch there, and cut the diagram at all height-critical points. The resulting finitely many open pieces are strictly height-monotone. Associate to each piece a closed interval of heights, whose endpoints are its two incident special heights. The interval has positive length: special heights are distinct, and a strictly monotone piece cannot return to its initial height. The desired rectangular replacement of a piece is a single vertical segment with precisely this interval. At an extremum, join its two incident segments by a horizontal cap. At a crossing, join the two underpassing incident segments by one horizontal segment crossing the continuing overpassing segment. No other horizontal segment is introduced. Thus the number of vertical pieces equals the number of horizontal joins, since every piece has two ends and every join has two incident ends. [given, construct]

2.1 Specify inequalities for the abscissae $x_i$ of the vertical pieces. Whenever two closed height intervals overlap in an interval with nonempty interior, prescribe their left-to-right order on a regular horizontal line in that overlap. This order is constant throughout the overlap: otherwise the two pieces would intersect, and an intersection is either an underpassing cut already made or a forbidden extra crossing. If intervals only meet at a special height, prescribe their order in the local cap or crossing picture. At a cap the two endpoints have the order of its two nearby branches. At a crossing, the two underpassing endpoints lie on opposite sides of the continuing overpassing piece, in the order given by the original crossing; all other pieces have their continued order outside that small crossing neighborhood. This gives a coherent total order on every collection of intervals containing a common height. In particular the two cap endpoints are consecutive among the pieces meeting its height, and at a crossing the only piece strictly between its underpassing endpoints is its overpassing piece. To see these last assertions, take a sufficiently small disk around the special point, disjoint from every other branch, and then a sufficiently close regular height: the incident branches are consecutive there except for the specified crossing branch. [step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 The directed inequalities in step 2.1 have no directed cycle. Here is the finite interval argument, including endpoint intersections. Three pairwise intersecting closed real intervals have a common point: the largest left endpoint does not exceed the smallest right endpoint. Thus the orders on any triangle are consistent by step 2.1. The intersection graph of finitely many intervals has no induced cycle of length at least four. Indeed choose in such a cycle an interval with largest left endpoint. Its two cycle neighbors both contain that endpoint, so they intersect each other and give a chord. If a shortest directed cycle had length at least four, this chord, in whichever direction its inequality points, would combine with one of the two directed paths around the cycle to give a shorter directed cycle. Length two is impossible, and length three was excluded. Hence the inequalities admit a total ordering: repeatedly remove a vertex with no incoming edge, which exists since following incoming edges indefinitely in a finite graph would give a cycle. Assign distinct integers in this order. They satisfy every prescribed strict inequality. [step 2.1, construct, cases, algebra]

4.1 Use these abscissae for the vertical segments and use the given special heights for the horizontal joins. Step 2.1 makes every cap disjoint from the other vertical segments and every crossing join meet exactly its designated overpassing segment. It also makes distinct joins disjoint, since their heights differ. The result is therefore an embedded decorated rectangular diagram except at the designated transverse vertical-over-horizontal crossings. Each vertical segment has exactly two incident horizontal ends, and no horizontal end lies in the interior of another segment. The incidence and orientations agree with the original link. A cap has no crossing and its two incident pieces lie on the same side in height; a crossing join has exactly one crossing and one incident piece above and one below. Consequently this diagram is bridge-like. Replace the ordered horizontal and vertical coordinates separately by consecutive grid coordinates, using increasing coordinate functions. Label the corners by their orientation: a corner where the oriented row starts is $O$ and where it ends is $X$. Every column then starts at $X$ and ends at $O$, so these labels give precisely [F1]. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 We verify that the smoothing has the asserted bridge class, rather than just the same undecorated incidence graph. Choose disjoint thin horizontal bands around the special heights. In the complement the diagram consists of ordered graphs $x=f_i(y)$ with nonzero height derivative; their order agrees with the ordered vertical segments. At a cap, the one-dimensional Morse coordinate is explicit: after translating its height, write $Y(q)=q^2a(q)$ with $a(0)>0$ (or its negative), and replace $q$ by $q\sqrt{a(q)}$. The two local branches are then indexed by $q=\pm\sqrt{|y|}$. At a crossing both branches are graphs in $y$ and their abscissa difference has a simple zero, because the tangents are transverse and neither is horizontal. Smooth the rectangular model in the bands so that it has the same critical heights, graph orders and crossing slopes, with the chosen underpassing branch passing through the crossing monotonically. Such smoothing is made by rounding each corner in a small empty disk and replacing each crossing join by a slightly tilted arc; its slope and height can be chosen so that the crossing is at the specified band center. For a cap, first prescribe its very small central neighborhood as a positive horizontal affine image of the original Morse cap, and join it to the two vertical legs by smooth monotone branches in the remaining empty cap neighborhood. This permits arbitrarily small height displacement of the horizontal cap, and ensures that the local matching below is affine with constant coefficients near its critical point. [step 2.1, step 4.1, given, construct]

6.1 For clarity, the ordered graph matching in step 5.1 gives an actual bridge isotopy. Near a crossing use the affine map of the horizontal coordinate matching the two graph values. Its slope is the quotient of their abscissa differences, hence extends smoothly and positively across their common simple zero. Near a cap use the constant-coefficient positive affine map prescribed in step 5.1. It is already defined on both sides of the critical height. Away from that central neighborhood the two branches are separated regular graphs, so no extension across a square-root singularity is needed. These local horizontal affine maps may be restricted to small disjoint neighborhoods. On the remaining compact regular bands all matching graph values have a positive separation. Extend the prescribed horizontal maps to increasing smooth diffeomorphisms on each fiber: between consecutive prescribed neighborhoods, choose a small positive constant derivative near the ends, interpolate the prescribed positive derivatives in smaller end collars, and add a nonnegative smooth bump in the gap to make the derivative integral equal the required positive image gap. Shrink the collars first so their integrals are smaller than that image gap. The lower separation bound makes this construction smooth in $y$; finite bands and smooth partitions in their overlapping $y$ intervals patch the maps by convex combinations. Such combinations still have positive horizontal derivative and still agree with all required graph values. Outside a large rectangle choose the identity, using the same gap construction. Thus there is a smooth family $h_y$ of increasing horizontal diffeomorphisms carrying one smoothed diagram to the other after an increasing reparameterization of their special heights. The maps $(x,y)\mapsto((1-t)x+t h_y(x),y)$ are plane diffeomorphisms and preserve all special heights and crossing decorations. Increasing reparameterizations of height are likewise isotopic to the identity through increasing functions. They prove bridge isotopy. All choices here are finite. [step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 The same interval pieces and inequalities are associated to every diagram in a bridge isotopy. Critical points and crossings continue uniquely, their height order cannot change, and their incidence, orientations and graph orders cannot change without a forbidden special-height coincidence or crossing degeneracy. Identify corresponding pieces once and for all. Any bridge-like rectangular diagram whose smoothing has this bridge class satisfies precisely these inequalities: its vertical segment gives the corresponding piece and its local horizontal cap or crossing gives the order at an interval endpoint. Conversely steps 4.1–6.1 realize every solution with distinct abscissae. The allowed height vectors form the convex cone $y_1<\cdots<y_N$; the allowed abscissa vectors form the open convex set defined by the finitely many strict inequalities $x_i<x_j$ from step 2.1. Thus two realizations can first have their heights moved to the same ordered values and then have their abscissa vectors joined within this convex set. Moving heights within their fixed order never changes the associated grid. [step 2.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, given, construct]

8.1 Choose a piecewise linear path between the two abscissa vectors which crosses the finitely many hyperplanes $x_i=x_j$ one at a time and transversely. This can be done within the open convex set by choosing one intermediate point outside the finitely many affine hyperplanes which would force a parallel or simultaneous intersection; a small ball inside the open set is not covered by finitely many proper affine hyperplanes, as is seen by restricting their defining polynomials to a generic line. Pairs whose intervals intersect have a prescribed strict inequality and can never meet on this path. Therefore each equality encountered is between pieces with disjoint closed vertical intervals. At the instant of equality they are adjacent in abscissa order, since simultaneous equalities were excluded. Their grid columns exchange by a legal disjoint-interval commutation. Between these finitely many instants both coordinate orders are fixed and the normalized grid is identical. This gives the claimed finite commutation sequence, with markings transported by the unchanged oriented incidence. No assertion about birth/death, crossing-slide, or Reidemeister events is needed for this lemma. [F1, step 3.1, step 7.1, construct, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $C$ be the Conway knot represented by Piccirillo's Figure 1 with its chosen orientation, and let $Q$ be the oriented knot with the following counterclockwise incoming-under PD (equal labels are joined):
$$[(38,82,39,81),(106,79,107,80),(57,81,58,80),(72,84,73,83),(91,82,92,83),(77,61,78,60),(78,103,79,104),(70,53,71,54),(44,73,45,74),(26,75,27,76),(7,77,8,76),(64,98,65,97),(52,69,53,70),(1,67,2,66),(32,67,33,68),(59,19,60,18),(37,56,38,57),(15,59,16,58),(50,96,51,95),(43,91,44,90),(28,47,29,48),(5,49,6,48),(42,23,43,24),(41,11,42,10),(31,97,32,96),(22,12,23,11),(12,22,13,21),(104,17,105,18),(9,88,10,89),(3,98,4,99),(84,46,85,45),(86,26,87,25),(93,55,94,54),(85,75,86,74),(87,8,88,9),(4,30,5,29),(51,34,52,35),(68,33,69,34),(94,36,95,35),(14,40,15,39),(99,47,100,46),(100,28,101,27),(101,6,102,7),(102,62,103,61),(65,3,66,2),(63,30,64,31),(62,49,63,50),(19,40,20,41),(20,14,21,13),(24,90,25,89),(55,109,56,108),(16,105,17,106),(92,109,93,0),(36,108,37,107),(71,1,72,0)].$$
Then there is an orientation-preserving smooth diffeomorphism $X_0(C)\cong X_0(Q)$ and the rational Lee filtration levels of $Q$ are $1,3$, so $s(Q)=2$. No identification of $Q$ with the named Figure 2 partner is part of this assertion.

## Statement references

[[def-piccirillo-conway-pair|The specified oriented Conway Figure 1 diagram]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice and the two specified finite diagrams.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed.

[F1] [[def-piccirillo-conway-pair]] specifies the literal Conway Figure 1 diagram. Its explicit eleven-crossing transcription, crossing centers and complete visit word are supplied by the direct Figure 1 calculation in [[lem-piccirillo-knot-lee-computations]], Proof 1.1. Only that diagram transcription is used in the trace construction, rather than an identification by an invariant.

[F2] [[def-handle-slide-of-one-k-handle-over-another]] and [[lem-handle-slides-preserve-the-relative-diffeomorphism-type]] supply framed equal-index slides and their relative diffeomorphisms.

[F3] [[lem-attaching-handles-along-isotopic-attaching-embeddings-preserves-the-diffeomorphism-type]] extends an isotopy of the complete framed attaching regions to a diffeomorphism of the attachments.

[F4] [[thm-handle-cancellation]] cancels an actual one-intersection consecutive pair. Its Proof 2.1 localizes the old-boundary support in the tube about the outside attaching arc together with the two feet.

[F5] [[alg-khovanov-chain-complex-from-diagram]] and [[def-lee-deformed-khovanov-complex]] give the normalized rational cube and its Lee perturbation. The zero smoothing joins PD positions $(0,1),(2,3)$ and the one smoothing joins $(0,3),(1,2)$.

[F6] [[lem-lee-filtered-spectral-sequence-and-two-orientation-classes]] and [[def-rasmussen-s-invariant]] give the two limiting knot levels, their difference two, and $s=s_{max}-1=s_{min}+1$. The possible nonzero Lee differentials change homological degree by one and quantum degree by $4k$, $k\ge1$.

[F7] The finite data used below are in the accompanying family file `alternate-trace-certificate.json.gz`, with its executable `verify-alternate-trace.py`. It contains all input PDs, every intermediate cyclic adjacency/under-over/color graph of the selected moves, explicit band polygons and ancestry, the I/J context map and cap coordinates, and the directly bound rational input/output. These are finite encodings, not additional topological assumptions. The proof describes their geometric interpretation.

[F8] [[lem-knot-exterior-h1-is-generated-by-meridian]] gives $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu_L]$ for each chosen knot tube and positive meridian. [[def-knot-meridian-and-preferred-longitude]] identifies a degree-one parallel with zero exterior-homology class as a preferred longitude.

[F9] [[thm-oriented-linking-number-scan-terminates-and-is-correct]] and [[lem-linking-number-even-sum-and-reidemeister-invariance]] give the integer mixed-crossing half-sum, invariant under oriented link isotopy. Its equality with the meridian coordinate is established in the local comparison below, by the same finite crossing-switch argument already used in the repaired generic dualizable-trace theorem; these suppliers alone are not claimed to assert that comparison.

## Proof

1.1 Interpret each finite movie in [F7] geometrically. Its records retain all four cyclic halfports, crossing height and component names. The checker verifies the actual monogon, opposite bigon, triangular-face and same-face premises for the indicated Reidemeister moves, and checks the complete resulting graph and every seam. A constant-over or constant-under record consists of a simple successive overstrand or understrand and the recorded simple dual-face replacement path: raise the arc into an empty upper slab or lower it into an empty lower slab, isotope the two boundary-parallel arcs there relative to their endpoint collars, and return. A finite polygonal sweep realizes this as an ambient isotopy. An orientation-preserving ribbon isomorphism at a seam is a planar isotopy of the finite projection graph, retaining every underpass; no reflection is permitted. Extend each motion to a sufficiently small normal tube and use [F3]. Thus every selected record is an actual framed attaching isotopy. The deterministic replay checks 2,129 such moves on their directly specified inputs; it compares complete diagrams, not invariants. [A1, F3, F7, construct]

2.1 Begin with source panel $F$: dotted red $R$, zero-framed green $G$, zero-framed blue $B$. Its complete 36-crossing PD has 16 blue self-crossings, 18 blue/red crossings and two green/red crossings, and no others. The actual red projection is simple, and green is its tiny meridian: choose disks $D_R,D_G$ meeting along a single radial slit, with $G\cap D_R$ one point, while $D_G$ misses the entire blue framed tube. To justify the initial cancellation, put blue transverse to $D_R$. At each blue puncture $p$, take a thin green zero-parallel bounding $D_G'$ disjoint from blue; its slit in $D_R$ is parallel to the fixed slit. The disk minus these two radial slits is connected. A simple disk arc from $p$ to the new puncture, avoiding the slits and all other punctures, thickens to an untwisted blue-over-green band. Push its new product arch across the empty bigon to the other side of $D_R$. This reduces the actual puncture count by one and preserves disjointness from $D_G$. Induction clears the finite set, so [F4] cancels $R,G$ off the blue tube. After these components are forgotten, each band together with $D_G'$ is an embedded product bigon disjoint from the current blue tube; reversing these disk pushes identifies the remaining blue knot with the original literal blue $B$. Because $f(G)=\operatorname{lk}(B,G)=0$ throughout, its transported framing stays zero. The input-bound 98-move blue movie and the 7-move source-Conway movie in [F7] identify this $B$ with the eleven-crossing Figure 1 input. The latter has visit word $U2,O8,U7,U11,O10,O9,U6,O2,U5,O7,U9,O6,U8,O5,O4,U3,O1,U4,O11,U10,O3,U1$ in the literal crossing-center order, so it is the specified $C$. Thus the $F$ handlebody is $X_0(C)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

2.2 To relate these framing integers to the zero-trace longitude, fix any disjoint oriented components $L,J$ with the chosen tube. Write $[J]=m[\mu_L]$ by [F8]; radial retraction in the punctured tube identifies the same coordinate in $S^3\setminus L$. Let $\ell$ be their diagram mixed-crossing half-sum from [F9]. ## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. In the oriented projection plane with coordinates $(x,y)$ and viewing normal $+z$, put $O_r=(r+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ and $X_r=((r+2)\bmod5+\frac12,r+\frac12)$ for $0\le r<5$. Join each row by its straight planar segment oriented from $O$ to $X$, each column by its straight planar segment oriented from $X$ to $O$, and put vertical segments over horizontal segments. After rounding the corners, the resulting oriented knot is ambient isotopic in the standard oriented three-sphere to the canonical complex torus knot $T(2,-3)$. It is therefore the mirror, and also the reverse mirror, of $T(2,3)$ with the canonical orientations. This identifies the exact five-grid used in the finite filtered staircase calculation, without inferring knot type from a homology calculation.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[def-coprime-torus-knot]]

[[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]]

[[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The explicit finite planar grid and the ambient and crossing conventions in the Statement.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]] is assumed for the smooth uniqueness conclusion of [F2].

[F1] [[def-planar-diagram-gauss-and-dowker-codes]] records an over-visit positively and an under-visit negatively in a cyclic Gauss word, separately from the determinant crossing sign. At a negative crossing the clockwise dart order beginning with the outgoing over-dart is $(O_{\rm out},U_{\rm out},O_{\rm in},U_{\rm in})$.

[F2] [[thm-valid-code-reconstructs-the-declared-link-diagram]] proves smooth planar isotopy uniqueness for diagrams with the same full signed rotation, pairing, orientation and outer-face code. Its actual proof constructs matching crossing neighborhoods and edge strips, extends over the face disks with prescribed collars, and joins the resulting plane diffeomorphism to the identity.

[F3] [[lem-choice-free-isotopy-extension-for-a-compact-smooth-source]] extends a smooth isotopy of a compact embedded source to an ambient isotopy supported near its track.

[F4] [[def-coprime-torus-knot]] fixes $T(p,q)$ as $(r e^{ipu},\sqrt{1-r^2}e^{iqu})$, $u\in\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, and fixes the mirror by conjugating the second complex coordinate.

## Proof

1.1 Translate the grid by $(-\frac12,-\frac12)$ so its marks have integer coordinates. The component follows the rows in order $0,2,4,1,3,0$, since each horizontal segment goes from row $r$ to column $r+2$ modulo five and the next vertical endpoint is $O_{r+2}$. It is consequently one knot. The horizontal open segments have endpoints $(r,r)$ and $((r+2)\bmod5,r)$. Column $c$ has endpoints $(c,(c-2)\bmod5)$ and $(c,c)$. Testing strict interior containment gives exactly three crossings, $A=(2,1)$, $B=(3,2)$ and $C=(1,3)$. At $A,B$ the over- and under-tangents are respectively $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$; at $C$ they are $(0,-1)$ and $(-1,0)$. All determinants are $-1$. Traversing from $O_0$, the column at $x=2$ visits $A$ over, row $2$ visits $B$ under, column $1$ visits $C$ over, row $1$ visits $A$ under, column $3$ visits $B$ over, and row $3$ visits $C$ under. Thus the signed visit word is $(+A,-B,+C,-A,+B,-C)$ and the crossing-sign vector is $(-1,-1,-1)$. Corners can be rounded in disjoint disks missing the crossings, so these are the exact smooth diagram data. [given, F1, construct, algebra]

1.2 Put $r=s=1/\sqrt2$ and consider the explicit complex torus curve $\kappa(u)=(r e^{2iu},s e^{-3iu})$. Use stereographic coordinates $\Psi(z_1,z_2)=(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2)/(1-\operatorname{Im}z_2)$. The removed point is not on this torus. This chart preserves the standard boundary orientation of $S^3\subset\mathbb C^2$: at $(0,0,0,-1)$ its positive tangent basis is $(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{y_1},\partial_{x_2})$, and the chart derivative is a positive scalar on this basis. The planar projection of $\Psi\kappa$ has polar angle $2u$, radius $\rho(u)=r/(1+s\sin3u)$, and height $Z(u)=s\cos3u/(1+s\sin3u)$. Two distinct parameters project to the same point only if they differ by $\pi$, because $\rho>0$. Equality of their radii then says $\sin3u=0$. Hence there are precisely three double points, with paired parameters $u=k\pi/3$ and $u+\pi$. They have distinct polar angles and no triple points. At an even $k$, the first parameter has height $+s$ and is over; its partner has height $-s$. In the positive radial/angular frame their tangents are $(-3rs,2r)$ and $(3rs,2r)$, of determinant $-12r^2s<0$. In particular every double point is transverse and negative. Starting at $u=0$, label the first three visits $A,B,C$. The six visits give exactly $(+A,-B,+C,-A,+B,-C)$, with sign vector $(-1,-1,-1)$. This proves the code equality directly from the canonical torus embedding, not from a knot table. [F1, F4, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The pairing joins each outgoing visit to the incoming dart of the next visit in that word. Together with the negative clockwise order of [F1], its face cycles are $(A O_{\rm out},B O_{\rm in})$, $(A U_{\rm out},C U_{\rm out},B U_{\rm out})$, $(A O_{\rm in},C O_{\rm out})$, $(A U_{\rm in},B U_{\rm in},C U_{\rm in})$ and $(B O_{\rm out},C O_{\rm in})$. Thus the connected graph has three vertices, six edges, and five faces, with three bigons and two triangles. Both actual diagrams realize this same oriented spherical rotation code, including every over/under pair and strand arrow. Choose matching faces as outer faces. If their original outer-face choices differ, regard each diagram on the sphere obtained by compactifying its projection plane, rotate a point of the required complementary face to infinity, and project again. This does not change the oriented link: put its diagram lift in a small collar of this standard equatorial sphere in $S^3$; rotations of the sphere extend to rotations of its ambient four-dimensional Euclidean space fixing the normal coordinate, and hence give explicit ambient isotopies of $S^3$. The normal collar coordinate retains the over/under inequalities. The resulting plane diagrams have the same full code with the same chosen outer face. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, given, construct, algebra]

3.1 Apply [F2] to these two diagrams. It gives an orientation-preserving smooth planar isotopy carrying every oriented edge and crossing decoration to its matching edge and decoration. Lift this family by retaining the third coordinate. On a compact neighborhood of the lifted diagram its track is compact; [F3] applied to a closed rounded three-dimensional neighborhood extends this family to an ambient isotopy of $S^3$. Finally two lifts of the same decorated projection are isotopic by linearly interpolating their height functions after matching their oriented parameters. Distinct projection points remain distinct; at a crossing the over-height minus the under-height stays strictly positive under this interpolation. The projected tangent never vanishes, so every interpolated curve is a smooth embedding. Make the time parameter stationary near its endpoints and apply [F3] to its compact circle source. This identifies the actual grid lift with $\Psi\kappa$, preserving orientation. By [F4] this is the claimed $T(2,-3)$. [A1, F2, F3, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Conjugation of the second complex coordinate sends the parametrized $T(2,3)$ to $\kappa$ with its image orientation, so the knot just identified is the prescribed mirror. It is also equivalent to the reverse of that mirror. Indeed simultaneous complex conjugation sends $\kappa(u)$ to $\kappa(-u)$. In real coordinates it fixes the two real axes and negates the two imaginary axes. This is the endpoint of the explicit rotations from angle zero to $\pi$ in the plane spanned by those imaginary axes, fixing the real axes. Every such rotation lies in $SO(4)$ and preserves $S^3$ and its orientation. The resulting ambient isotopy reverses the orientation along this specific knot at its terminal map. Therefore mirror and reverse mirror are oriented-isotopic in this case. Every assertion is geometric; no analytic comparison, Floer rank, tau value, or staircase identification is used. [F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. Use the actual based earring $K\cup L\subset S^3$, its normal radius arc $\omega$, the compact exterior $X$ and a supplied $SO(3)$ bundle $P\to X$ with $w_2(P)=PD_{\mathbb F_2}[\omega]$ in the singular-data definition. Both boundary-torus restrictions of $P$ have nonzero $w_2$. The bundle admits a compatible extension to an order-two orbifold bundle over $(S^3,K\cup L)$ whose local isotropy is rotation by $\pi$, whose axis-orientation cover on each link component is nontrivial, and whose ordinary local singular residue is $\frac14\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)d\theta$ up to conjugation. It therefore supplies the compatible finite local data required by the order-two gauge-completion lemma.

For this completed data every connection has determinant-one stabilizer exactly $\{\pm1\}$. The bundle on the exterior also has an actual $U(2)$ lift with a chosen determinant line and determinant connection, as needed for cylinder holonomy functions. These statements concern the topology and analytic input data, not independence of the resulting choices or construction of Floer homology. The supplied-bundle existence clause of the original definition is retained; this result does not classify all singular extensions up to canonical isomorphism.

## Statement references

[[def-singular-instanton-knot-and-sutured-closure-data]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, §§2.2, 3.1–3.3 and4.2–4.3](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/khovanov-unknot.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] The earring arc has exactly one endpoint on each boundary torus and is normal there. Integral and mod-two Poincare–Lefschetz cap duality have coefficient-compatible chain formulas. [[def-singular-instanton-knot-and-sutured-closure-data]] [[thm-poincare-lefschetz-duality]]

[F2] The actual Spin lifting proof identifies the local triple-sign cocycle of lifts through $SU(2)\to SO(3)$ with the defined characteristic class $w_2$, for every oriented rank-three bundle. Its cell-boundary comparison also identifies the obstruction on an oriented two-cell with the parity of its quaternionic lifted clutching loop. [[lem-spin-structures-exist-iff-w2-vanishes-and-form-h1-torsor]]

[F3] The quaternionic cover has kernel $\{\pm1\}$ and $\pi_2(SO(3))=0$. Finite good covers of this compact exterior compute integral and mod-two cohomology compatibly and have smooth subordinate partitions. [[lem-the-second-homotopy-group-of-so-three-vanishes]] [[lem-finite-good-covers-of-compact-smooth-boundary-manifolds-compute-integral-cohomology]]

[F4] Integral degree-two classes are first Chern classes of actual line bundles. The finite invariant analytic completion and gauge regularity are constructed in the preceding analytic supplier. Full AC is inherited through these suppliers. [[thm-first-chern-class-classifies-complex-line-bundles]] [[lem-order-two-singular-gauge-completions-and-cylindrical-fredholm-operators]] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]



## Proof

**Given:** Full AC and the supplied exterior bundle in the Statement, without assuming an already constructed singular extension.

1.1 **The exact two boundary obstructions.** Push either boundary torus slightly into $X$. It intersects the truncated radius arc once modulo two, because that arc has one endpoint on that torus and its product boundary collar is normal. The cap formula of [F1] therefore gives $\langle w_2(P),[T_K]\rangle=\langle w_2(P),[T_L]\rangle=1$. Orient the arc from its endpoint on $K$ to its endpoint on $L$. Its integral relative class gives $c=PD_{\mathbb Z}[\omega]\in H^2(X;\mathbb Z)$, whose reduction is $w_2(P)$ by the same coefficient-compatible cap formula. No integral lift is inferred merely from an evenness or torsion-free assertion. [F1, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 **An explicit orbifold solid torus with this obstruction.** Write its lifted local coordinates as $(t,z)\in\mathbb R\times D^2$. On the trivial adjoint bundle impose the two actions $(t,z,v)\mapsto(t,-z,ivi^{-1})$ and $(t,z,v)\mapsto(t+2\pi,z,jvj^{-1})$. Their base actions commute and their adjoint fiber actions commute, since $ij=-ji$ and central signs act trivially. They therefore define a smooth order-two orbifold $SO(3)$ bundle over the solid torus, with the product connection. On its boundary its meridional and longitudinal holonomies are $\operatorname{Ad}i$ and $\operatorname{Ad}j$. The lifted commutator $iji^{-1}j^{-1}=-1$ makes its $w_2$ evaluate to one by [F2]. The meridional fixed axis is $\mathbb Ri$, and its longitudinal transport reverses this axis, so the axis cover of the core circle is nontrivial. In a meridional double angular cover $\theta=2\phi$, the gauge $u(\phi)=\exp(-\phi\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)/2)$ is single-valued in $SO(3)$; it changes under the deck involution by the adjoint of $\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)$. Transforming between its smooth lifted product frame and an ordinary punctured-tube frame gives exactly residue $\frac14\operatorname{diag}(i,-i)d\theta$, with the opposite sign conjugate by $j$. Thus this is the prescribed local singular model, not a smooth ordinary filling of the original exterior bundle. [F2, F3, F4, construct, algebra]

2.1 **Actual boundary identifications and global gluing.** Oriented rank-three bundles on the two-torus with the same $w_2$ are isomorphic. For a direct verification, use its one-vertex, two-edge, one-face cell structure. A bundle is trivial on the one-skeleton since $SO(3)$ is connected. Compare its boundary frame around the face with a frame on that face's disk. Its parity in $\pi_1SO(3)=\mathbb Z/2$ is exactly $w_2$ by [F2]. For two equal parities, an isomorphism over the one-skeleton has a boundary discrepancy loop of parity zero, hence a closed lift to $S^3$, which contracts; extending this contraction across the face supplies an actual isomorphism. Approximate it smoothly in bundle homomorphism charts and polar-normalize; compactness preserves invertibility and positive determinant. Apply this to each boundary restriction in step 1.1 and the model in step 1.2. Glue the two model solid tori to $P$ along collars using these actual isomorphisms. Their overlaps are free orbifold regions, so the lifted local transition maps give ordinary smooth compatible maps there. Finite normal and exterior charts now supply the finite compatible orbifold chart/bundle atlas. Average lifted local positive metrics and model connections with a finite invariant partition, agreeing with the displayed model in smaller core neighborhoods. This gives an actual metric and smooth model connection for the completion lemma, with the required residue and nontrivial axis covers. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 **No determinant-one stabilizers have been hidden.** Let $u$ preserve any connection of this completion. The equation $d_Au=0$ implies it is a parallel unit-quaternion section; Sobolev gauge regularity in [F4] and the first-order equation make its lifted representatives continuous at the core and as regular as the connection. At a core point its invariance under the isotropy $i$ puts its value in the circle $\{a+bi:a^2+b^2=1\}$. Along the core the tangent connection form lies in the invariant axis algebra $\mathbb Ri$, so continuous parallel transport preserves that circle and acts trivially on it. But going once around the core includes the prescribed longitudinal transition $j$, which sends $a+bi$ to $a-bi$. Thus parallel invariance forces $b=0$ and $u=\pm1$. A parallel section is determined everywhere on the connected regular locus by its value at a point; using a radial path off the core gives the same conclusion on the whole bundle. Both central signs really are gauge stabilizers. This proves the all-connections hypothesis required by the critical-set supplier, not just absence of reducible flat connections. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **The actual exterior determinant lift.** Choose the finite good cover from [F3] refining bundle trivializations, and lift its $SO(3)$ transitions $g_{ij}$ to smooth unit quaternions $s_{ij}$ on the contractible overlaps. Write $s_{ij}s_{jk}s_{ki}=(-1)^{e_{ijk}}$; [F2] says $[e]=w_2(P)$. Represent the integral lift $c$ of step 1.1 by an integer nerve cocycle. Its reduction and $e$ differ by a mod-two coboundary, so changing the signs of $s_{ij}$ makes $e=c\bmod2$ as cochains. ## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $G$ be a nonempty bridge-like rectangular diagram, with the vertical-over convention and grid markings of the grid-diagram definition. Choose a vertical piece $P$, whose lower and upper endpoint rows are $L<T$, and choose a height $h\in(L,T)$ distinct from all horizontal levels. There is a finite sequence of two stabilizations and legal row commutations producing another bridge-like rectangular diagram. Its smoothing has the same bridge data as the original except for the insertion of a pair of nondegenerate height extrema near $h$ on the chosen piece. No crossing is added, removed, or redecorated, and all old special heights retain their order. A permitted stabilization duplicates its chosen marking type at opposite corners of a new two-by-two block, puts the other type at a third corner and leaves the last empty, preserving one of each type per row and column; adjacent rows with disjoint or strictly nested closed horizontal marking intervals may commute. Either side of the strand and either orientation are allowed. Reversing the sequence realizes the death.

Consequently, if two nonempty oriented bridge diagrams differ by a single ordinary local birth/death of height-critical points, their bridge rectifications are related by grid moves. This conclusion uses no grid-isotopy generation theorem or crossing-slide realization.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, the finite bridge-like rectangular diagram, its chosen vertical piece and regular height, or a single ordinary local bridge birth/death.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] fixes the row $O$-to-$X$, column $X$-to-$O$, and vertical-over conventions.

[F2] [[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]] gives rectifications of nonempty bridge diagrams and commutation equivalences between all rectifications with bridge-isotopic smoothings.

## Proof

1.1 Let $a$ be the type of the mark at $(P,L)$, and write $b$ for the other type. The mark at $(P,T)$ has type $b$. Choose real coordinates representing the grid orders. Insert a new column $Q$ immediately to the right of $P$ and a new row $H$ immediately above $L$. Stabilize at $(P,L)$ by removing its $a$ and putting $$a\text{ at }(P,H),\qquad b\text{ at }(Q,H),\qquad a\text{ at }(Q,L).$$ In the new block with north row $H$, south row $L$, west column $P$, east column $Q$, the northwest and southeast corners have $a$, the northeast has $b$, and the southwest is empty. This is an allowed stabilization. Row $L$ retains its unchanged exterior $b$, column $P$ retains its $b$ at $T$, and column $Q$ contains $b,a$. All rows and columns therefore still have exactly one of each marking. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 The short row $H$ has horizontal interval $[P,Q]$. Every original row strictly between $L$ and $T$ has both endpoints outside this interval: no old column was inserted between $P,Q$, the only original rows incident to $P$ are $L,T$, and $Q$ is new. Hence such a row has interval either disjoint from $[P,Q]$ or containing it in its interior. Move $H$ upward, one adjacent row at a time, until it lies in the gap containing $h$. Each exchange is a legal disjoint-interval or strictly nested-interval commutation. The labels of the other rows retain their relative order. No exchange with $L$ or $T$ is needed. If $h$ is already in the first gap the sequence is empty. Set the coordinate of the new $H$ inside the desired gap; coordinates within a fixed order do not change a grid. [F1, step 1.1, given, construct, cases]

3.1 Insert another new column $R$ strictly between the adjacent columns $P,Q$ and another new row $K$ immediately below $H$, above every original row below $H$. Stabilize the $a$ at $(P,H)$ by removing it and putting $$a\text{ at }(P,K),\qquad b\text{ at }(R,K),\qquad a\text{ at }(R,H).$$ The northwest corner $(P,H)$ is empty; northeast and southwest have $a$, and southeast has $b$. This is the other indicated stabilization block. The unchanged $(Q,H)$ has type $b$. Column $P$ now pairs its $a$ at $K$ with its exterior $b$ at $T$; column $R$ pairs $b$ at $K$ with $a$ at $H$; column $Q$ still pairs $b$ at $H$ with $a$ at $L$. Rows $K,H$ have respectively $(a,b)$ and $(a,b)$ in their displayed columns. All untouched rows and columns retain their markings. These statements cover both $a=O$ and $a=X$ without an unoriented identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The part of the final diagram replacing the original vertical piece is, ignoring its traversal orientation, $$ (P,T)\longrightarrow(P,K)\longrightarrow(R,K)\longrightarrow(R,H)\longrightarrow(Q,H)\longrightarrow(Q,L).$$ Here $L<K<H<T$ and $P<R<Q$. Row $K$ is a local minimum: both incident vertical pieces extend upward. Row $H$ is a local maximum: both incident vertical pieces extend downward. Their intervals $[P,R]$ and $[R,Q]$ contain no other column, so neither cap contains a crossing. There is no original horizontal level between $K,H$. Thus these are exactly the two new height extrema. Every original horizontal segment below $K$ that crossed $P$ now crosses $Q$ instead, and every one above $H$ still crosses $P$. Indeed its endpoints are outside the adjacent original-to-new strip; containing $P$ in its interior is equivalent to containing $Q$ there. There is no original endpoint on $P$ except in rows $L,T$, which remain endpoints rather than crossings. All other old intersections are untouched. This proves the assertion about the crossing list, decorations and special-height order. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, cases]

5.1 The old lower endpoint row $L$ is still the same kind of cap or crossing join. Moving its endpoint from $P$ to the immediately neighboring new $Q$ cannot pass any old column. At $L$ the column $P$ no longer extends down to that row, so it cannot become an unwanted crossing of the expanded horizontal interval. At $T$ nothing has changed. All other old horizontal joins keep their type and crossing count by step 4.1. The final diagram is consequently bridge-like, not merely a general grid. Round its two new caps in disjoint small disks and keep their heights inside the gap around $h$. The new local arc runs monotonically in the horizontal direction after its corners are rounded, and its height along that arc decreases, increases, then decreases, or has the reverse traversal. It is therefore the side of an ordinary birth having two nondegenerate critical points. Its three monotone pieces have the same order as the two newly inserted caps; the old side is the single monotone piece. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 To identify the local event precisely, an ordinary birth has a horizontal regular tangent at the singular point and local height $y=u^3/3-\tau u$, after changes preserving the height orientation and a possible reversal of $u$. For $\tau<0$ it is monotone; for $\tau>0$ its two critical points are $u=\pm\sqrt\tau$, with distinct maximum and minimum values and three ordered monotone pieces between these values. The transverse coordinate $x$ is strictly monotone in $u$ on a sufficiently small event neighborhood, because the original planar curve is immersed. Hence there are exactly two possible horizontal orders for these three pieces. Our construction gives $P<R<Q$; insertion of the two new columns to the left of $P$ gives its reflection and the opposite order. Reflecting the displayed finite coordinate certificate preserves adjacency, interval disjointness and containment, all marking types, and vertical-over decorations; it is a recipe for the opposite-side operations, not an assertion that a grid is move-equivalent to its own reflection. The choice $a=O$ or $a=X$ gives either direction of traversal. Thus all ordinary oriented local birth models, and their reversed deaths, have been treated. [F1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, cases]

7.1 Finally take any two bridge diagrams related by a local birth/death. On the monotone side, [F2] supplies a bridge rectification. The event lies on one of its vertical pieces after the identification by bridge data; choose $h$ in the corresponding regular-height gap. Steps 1.1–6.1 produce a bridge-like grid whose smoothing has exactly the bridge data of the other side, with the appropriate horizontal order, orientation and crossing decorations. The fiberwise bridge-isotopy construction in [F2] identifies these smoothings with that side, and its uniqueness assertion connects the produced grid to every other rectification by commutations. Applying [F2] on the first side as well makes the conclusion independent of its initially chosen rectification. Every operation was finite; no global generation or analytic assertion was used. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Use planar grid markings with horizontal orientation from $O$ to $X$,
vertical orientation from $X$ to $O$, and vertical segments over horizontal
segments. An allowed commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns when
their closed marking intervals are disjoint or one is contained in the
interior of the other. A stabilization splits a row and column through a
chosen marked cell into two each; its new $2\times2$ block has three
markings, with the chosen type twice, the other type once, and one empty
corner, and every new row and column again has one marking of each type.
Destabilization is the inverse operation.

Suppose a finite planar grid has four consecutive columns, labeled in order
$P,L,Q,R$, and two consecutive rows $H<K$. Its markings on those rows are
exactly
$$H:\ (P,b),(Q,\bar b),\qquad K:\ (L,a),(R,\bar a),$$
where $a,b\in\{O,X\}$ and a bar denotes the other type. The other marking
of column $P$ is in a row $T>K$; the other markings of columns $L,Q,R$
are in rows strictly below $H$. These hypotheses describe an overpassing
cap with columns $L,R$ and an underpassing segment from $P$ to $Q$,
crossing its left leg. Rows outside this specified pattern and columns
outside this consecutive block are arbitrary.

Insert a row $J$ immediately below $H$ and a column $U$ immediately to the
right of $Q$. There is the following certificate, where a column or row
label follows its markings under a commutation:

| Stage | Column order in the active block | Active row order | Operation from the preceding stage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | $P,L,Q,R$ | $H<K$ | Initial pattern |
| 1 | $P,L,Q,U,R$ | $J<H<K$ | Stabilize at $(Q,H)$ |
| 2 | $P,L,Q,R,U$ | $J<H<K$ | Commute $U,R$ |
| 3 | $P,L,Q,R,U$ | $J<K<H$ | Commute $H,K$ |
| 4 | $L,Q,R,P,U$ | $J<K<H$ | Commute $P$ successively past $L,Q,R$ |
| 5 | $L,Q,R,P,U$ | $J<H<K$ | Commute $H,K$ |
| 6 | $L,Q,R,P$ | $J<K$ | Destabilize, deleting $H,U$ |

At stages 1–5 the active markings, with their row and column labels, are
$$H:\ (P,b),(U,\bar b),\quad J:\ (Q,\bar b),(U,b),\quad K:\ (L,a),(R,\bar a).$$
At stage 6 they are
$$J:\ (Q,\bar b),(P,b),\qquad K:\ (L,a),(R,\bar a).$$
All other markings are transported by the stated row or column operations.
Thus the final underpassing segment crosses the right leg of the cap.
The six displayed arrows are $S,C,C,C,C,S^{-1}$, with the fourth arrow
comprising three elementary commutations. All four choices of $(a,b)$ are
valid whenever the initial markings extend to the given oriented grid.
Applying horizontal or vertical reflection to the entire certificate gives
the corresponding opposite-side or minimum pattern, with vertical segments
still over.

This is a conditional finite grid certificate for the specified over-arch
patterns. It does not assert that every bridge approximation has these
adjacency hypotheses, or that a crossing slide whose height-critical branch
is underpassing has been treated.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, FigureB.22](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite grid with the consecutive-column, consecutive-row, marking, and exterior-partner hypotheses of the statement.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] supplies one $O$ and one $X$ per row and column, horizontal orientation $O$ to $X$, vertical orientation $X$ to $O$, and vertical-over crossing data.

## Proof

1.1 Coordinates in the table specify only the order of row and column levels. Replacing finitely many distinct levels by their ranks does not change the marked grid, so the table can be checked using any increasing real coordinates. The other markings in columns $P,L,Q,R$ have complementary types $\bar b,\bar a,b,a$ respectively by [F1]. The new row $J$, being inserted immediately below $H$, remains above all three lower partner rows. The top partner row $T$ remains above $K$ and $H$ throughout the indicated row interchanges. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Stabilize the marking $\bar b$ at $(Q,H)$ by replacing it with $\bar b$ at $(U,H)$, $\bar b$ at $(Q,J)$, and $b$ at $(U,J)$. The cell $(Q,H)$ is empty. In the block with north row $H$, south row $J$, west column $Q$, and east column $U$, its northwest cell is empty, northeast and southwest have $\bar b$, and southeast has $b$. Row $H$ still pairs $b$ with $\bar b$, row $J$ pairs $\bar b$ with $b$, column $Q$ still pairs $\bar b$ with its unchanged exterior $b$, and column $U$ pairs $\bar b$ with $b$. All other rows and columns retain their two types. This is exactly a stabilization of type $\bar b:\mathrm{NW}$ and gives stage 1. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 At stage 1, the closed vertical interval of $U$ is $[J,H]$. The interval of $R$ starts at its lower partner row and ends at $K$. Its endpoints satisfy $\text{lower partner}<J<H<K$, so $[J,H]$ lies strictly inside it. The two columns are adjacent by their order in the table. Their exchange is an allowed nested-interval commutation and gives stage 2. This reasoning does not depend on either marking type. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 At stage 2, row $H$ has endpoints $P,U$ and row $K$ has endpoints $L,R$. The column order is $P<L<Q<R<U$, so $[L,R]$ lies strictly inside $[P,U]$. The rows are adjacent. Their exchange is therefore an allowed nested-interval commutation, giving stage 3. [step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 At stage 3 the vertical interval of $P$ is $[H,T]$. Those of $L,R$ end at $K<H$, and that of $Q$ ends at $J<H$; all begin at their lower partner rows. Hence each is disjoint as a closed interval from $[H,T]$. Commute $P$ with its adjacent neighbor $L$, then with $Q$, then with $R$. At each exchange these same labeled intervals remain disjoint, and the adjacent-column orders are successively $L,P,Q,R,U$, $L,Q,P,R,U$, and $L,Q,R,P,U$. This proves the fourth table arrow as three allowed commutations, not a single nonadjacent-column move. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 At stage 4 the closed horizontal intervals of rows $K,H$ are respectively $[L,R]$ and $[P,U]$. The column order $L<Q<R<P<U$ makes them disjoint, including their endpoints. They are adjacent rows. Their exchange is an allowed disjoint-interval commutation and gives stage 5, with $J<H<K$. [step 2.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 At stage 5 the adjacent rows $J,H$ and adjacent columns $P,U$ contain $b$ in $(P,H)$ and $(U,J)$, $\bar b$ in $(U,H)$, and an empty $(P,J)$. The other marking in row $J$ is $\bar b$ in column $Q$ outside this block, and the other marking in column $P$ is $\bar b$ in row $T$ outside it. Thus this is a $b:\mathrm{SW}$ stabilization block in reverse. Contract it, deleting row $H$ and column $U$, and put $b$ in $(P,J)$. The remaining marking $(Q,J)$ has type $\bar b$. Every retained row and column again has one marking of each type. This proves stage 6 and the claimed finite move word. The only altered exterior coordinates are exactly those moved by the stated full row and column exchanges; nothing about arbitrary exterior markings was assumed. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Initially the horizontal $H$ segment between $P$ and $Q$ crosses column $L$, whose upper endpoint is at $K>H$, but not column $R$. Finally the $J$ segment between $Q$ and $P$ crosses column $R$, whose upper endpoint is at $K>J$, but not $L$. The overpassing cap consists of the vertical legs $L,R$ and their horizontal segment at $K$; the relative order of the three lower legs $L,Q,R$ is retained. If $a=O$ the cap is oriented from its left lower leg to its right lower leg, and if $a=X$ the direction reverses. If $b=O$ the other strand enters from row $T$ and exits down column $Q$, and if $b=X$ this direction reverses. Every new corner's type is already prescribed in steps 2.1 and 7.1, so these four orientation cases require no unmarked or unoriented identification. Reflecting the entire labeled certificate horizontally or vertically preserves adjacency, disjointness, and strict interval containment and takes a three-mark stabilization block to another allowed such block. It also preserves which segments are vertical and hence which are over. It therefore supplies the stated opposite-side and minimum certificates; this does not assert a grid-move equivalence from a grid to its own reflection. Axis exchange is not used. The result is precisely the conditional finite certificate stated, with no claim about underpassing critical branches or general bridge rectification. Every operation is finite and needs no choice axiom. [F1, step 2.1, step 7.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let two nonempty oriented bridge diagrams differ by one crossing sliding through one nondegenerate height extremum of a branch. The other branch is not height-critical, the crossing decorations are unchanged, and no other special height lies between these two interacting special heights on either sufficiently close side. Then any ordinary bridge-like grid rectifications of the two sides are connected by finitely many marked stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations, with the row $O$-to-$X$, column $X$-to-$O$, and vertical-over conventions. The height-critical branch may be overpassing or underpassing, and every orientation and maximum/minimum variant is included. No condition is imposed on the exterior strands or their remote endpoint heights.

A legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. The stabilizations and destabilizations are the usual three-mark two-by-two split and its inverse. In particular a shared-endpoint switch is not taken as a primitive grid move. No global grid-isotopy generation assertion is used.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]]

[[lem-grid-regular-jog-refinements]]

[[lem-grid-bridge-crossing-slide-realization]]

[[lem-grid-underpassing-bridge-crossing-slide-realization]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The bridge crossing slide, with its local decorated and oriented branches, and the finite grid-move conventions in the statement.

[F1] [[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]] gives ordinary rectifications and their commutation equivalence within a bridge-isotopy class.

[F2] [[lem-grid-regular-jog-refinements]] gives exact marked interior vertical-piece splitting by a stabilization and short-row sweep, and removal of all crossing-free regular jogs to an ordinary rectification by actual grid moves.

[F3] [[lem-grid-bridge-crossing-slide-realization]] gives the overpassing-cap certificate on consecutive columns $P,L,Q,R$ and consecutive rows $H<K$, with $P$'s other mark above $K$ and the other marks of $L,Q,R$ below $H$. It tracks all exterior markings.

[F4] [[lem-grid-underpassing-bridge-crossing-slide-realization]] gives the underpassing-cap certificate on consecutive columns $L,B,M,R$ and rows $H<K$, with the other marks of $L,R$ below $H$ and the two marks of $B$ outside $[H,K]$. It decomposes its shared-endpoint row switch into permitted moves and tracks all exterior markings.

## Proof

1.1 Take an ordinary bridge rectification of the first side using [F1]. Initially its designated columns need not be consecutive. For an overpassing maximum, write its cap row as $K$ with legs $L<R$, and its nearby crossing row as $H<K$. The crossing-containing underpassing join has one endpoint outside the cap and one inside. Its upper incident piece must be outside: an inside upper piece would continue above $K$, since no special height intervenes, and would cross the allegedly empty cap. By horizontal reflection of the coordinate recipe and, if necessary, reversing the move, the column order is $P<L<Q<R$, with $P$ the upper incident piece and $Q$ the lower one. Thus its row and partner data are those of [F3], except for column consecutiveness. For an underpassing maximum, the overpassing branch continues through the whole band as one vertical piece $B$, while the underpassing branch has a short piece $M$ between its crossing row $H$ and cap row $K$. The same empty-cap test puts these columns in order $L<B<M<R$, up to the same choices of side and move direction. These are exactly the non-adjacency parts of [F4]. The two rows are consecutive because no other special height intervenes. [F1, given, construct, cases]

2.1 Every other original column strictly between the leftmost and rightmost of the four designated columns has its entire closed vertical interval below $H$ or above $K$. In the overpassing case a column present at height $K$ between $L,R$ would cross the empty cap. A column between $P,L$ present at $H$ would add a second crossing to row $H$. The same argument covers the remaining subintervals, using the empty cap or the fact that the crossing row contains exactly its designated crossing. Since no old marking row is strictly between $H,K$, a foreign interval cannot meet just one interior part of the band without containing $H$ or $K$. Its endpoints cannot equal $H,K$, whose marks are already the four designated endpoints. For the underpassing case, the cap $[M,R]$ and the one-crossing join $[L,M]$ give the identical exclusion. Thus all foreign intervals in the relevant column span miss the entire closed band. [step 1.1, given, construct, cases]

2.2 Let $H_-$ be the old row immediately below $H$ and $K_+$ the old row immediately above $K$; if either is absent use an arbitrary exterior level on that side. Each lower incident designated piece has its other endpoint in a row at or below $H_-$. In the overpassing case these lower pieces are $L,Q,R$, in that left-to-right order. Split them by [F2], inserting a new lower anchor column immediately right of each original column and moving its crossing-free jog row to heights $$H_-<j_L<j_Q<j_R<H.$$ The original columns now contain only the upper pieces beginning at these cut rows; the new lower anchor for $C$ has interval ending at $j_C$. In the underpassing case do the same for $L,B,R$ with $$H_-<j_L<j_B<j_R<H.$$ The short column $M$ is not cut. All new row levels lie in the formerly empty gap, and all mark types are exactly those prescribed in [F2], with the original lower-end type used separately on each piece. The sweeps remain legal even past an earlier inserted cut row, since the two columns of the newly inserted jog are adjacent and the earlier row has neither endpoint on them. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Cut the unique upper incident piece as well: it is $P$ in the first case and $B$ in the second. If its upper mark has type $d$ in row $T$, insert an anchor immediately right of its column and a row $i$ immediately below $T$, replace the old mark by $d$ in the original column at $i$, $\bar d$ in the anchor at $i$, and $d$ in the anchor at $T$. With north row $T$ and south row $i$, northwest is empty, northeast and southwest have $d$, and southeast has $\bar d$, so this is an allowed stabilization. Sweep the short row downward to $$K<i<K_+$$ by the same disjoint-or-strictly-nested test as in [F2]. The original upper piece is now bounded above by $i$, while its upper anchor starts at $i$. For $B$ this is done after its lower cut, so its localized interval is $[j_B,i]$. Each old foreign interval in step 2.1 is either below every lower cut or above $i$, since its endpoints are old row levels. [F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 Bring the four localized original columns together, preserving their order, by moving each of them left past intervening inactive columns, one adjacent exchange at a time. Every such exchange has disjoint closed intervals. Foreign old columns are disjoint from every localized piece by the preceding three cut and exclusion constructions. The upper anchor, if before a later localized column, starts above $K$, while that later column ends at or below $K$. A lower anchor for a designated piece can occur before a later lower localized piece only in the same left-to-right order used for the cut heights; its interval ends at an earlier $j$, strictly below that later piece's lower cut. In the underpassing case it may also precede the short $M$, whose interval starts at $H$ and is therefore disjoint from every lower anchor. No exchange of inactive columns with each other is needed: this is the finite stable sorting which puts the four distinguished letters before all intervening inactive letters while retaining the order within each list. Every inversion just enumerated is disjoint. The four localized columns are now consecutive and in the original designated order. The rows $H,K$ remain consecutive. [step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, construct, cases]

5.1 Apply [F3] or [F4] to this actual grid. Its hypotheses now hold literally. Lower partner heights are the cut rows below $H$, the unique upper partner is $i>K$, and the short $M$ has its original two endpoint rows. The certificates give genuine finite grid moves, not switches as extra primitives. In the overpassing case the four surviving localized columns end in order $L,Q,R,P$. The relative order of the lower incident pieces $L,Q,R$ is unchanged. In the underpassing case they end in order $L,M,B,R$, and the relative order of the lower incident pieces $L,B,R$ is unchanged. The unique upper incident piece is the same in either case. Rename the surviving crossing and cap levels $H,K$: the certificate inserts levels only immediately beside the interacting levels, so the new crossing remains above every lower cut and the cap below the upper cut. Every original marking outside the localized columns and interacting rows is transported exactly as asserted by those certificates. [F3, F4, step 4.1, construct, cases]

6.1 Check the cut rows after the certificate, since they cannot be dismissed as harmless without proof. At a lower cut row $j_C$, the jog joins its localized column to its lower anchor, which remains in the inactive list to the right of all four localized columns. A later lower localized piece starts at a strictly larger cut height and is absent at $j_C$; an earlier lower localized piece is to the left of $C$, in both the initial and final orders. A lower anchor with an earlier cut ends below $j_C$, and an anchor with a later cut lies after $C$'s anchor in the retained inactive order. The short $M$, when present, starts at $H>j_C$, and the upper-only piece $P$, when present, also starts at $H$. Upper anchors and old foreign columns are absent at all these cut heights. Thus no vertical segment lies in the interior of the cut row's horizontal interval. At the upper cut $i$, all other localized pieces end at or below $K$, all lower anchors end below $H$, and every old foreign upper interval begins at or above $K_+>i$; that jog is empty too. Each cut jog is monotone, because its two incident legs run respectively into the lower and upper parts of the same original oriented strand. All these statements remain true after the local column permutations, because the lower-piece order was retained in step 5.1. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, cases]

7.1 Every old horizontal row outside $H,K$ lies outside the localized vertical range, except for the newly inserted cut rows just checked. Its markings and crossing order therefore cannot acquire an extra crossing from the local certificates. Its old upper or lower continuation is carried by the same inactive anchor as before. The two interacting rows have exactly the cap and crossing patterns on the other side of the slide, by [F3] or [F4]. Consequently the output is a generalized bridge rectification: it has the original exterior bridge data, the desired new local bridge data, and only the empty monotone jogs of step 6.1. Its oriented strand incidence and crossing decorations agree with the desired second diagram. The ordered-graph bridge-isotopy construction in [F1] identifies these data; for regular jogs its exact extension is included in [F2]. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 5.1, step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Remove all regular jogs using [F2]. It supplies an actual finite move sequence to an ordinary bridge-like grid of the second bridge-isotopy class. Finally [F1] connects that grid to any prescribed rectification of the second side, and likewise permits any initial rectification. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 7.1, construct, cases] ∎
