## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Use a size-$n\ge2$ toroidal grid, its flat oriented torus $T=\mathbb R^2/(n\mathbb Z)^2$, horizontal alpha circles and vertical beta circles, and $X=\operatorname{Sym}^n(T)$. At each generator use the actual flat product chart with alpha plane $\mathbb R^n$ and beta plane $i\mathbb R^n$. The path of target almost complex structures may be any homotopy of the standard complex structure compatible with these boundary planes and fixed product ends as in the relative-index suppliers.

For each embedded grid rectangle $R$ from $x$ to $y$, with $x$ at its northeast and southwest corners and with no other point of $x$ in its interior, there is an actual continuous Whitney class $r_R:x\to y$ whose domain is exactly $R$ and whose actual fixed-end Fredholm index is $1$. Markings inside $R$ are unrestricted.

For every generator $x$ and every closed band between consecutive horizontal grid circles there is an actual based disk on $L_\alpha$, based at $x$, with domain that unit row annulus and boundary Maslov index $2$. Likewise every consecutive column annulus is the domain of an actual based disk on $L_\beta$ with boundary Maslov index $2$. Inserting either disk on the corresponding boundary of the constant Whitney class at $x$ gives a class $x\to x$ of actual fixed-end index $2$. Reversals give the negative domains and negative indices, and finite concatenations are actual classes with additive domains and indices.

All these assertions construct classes and compute their linearized indices. They do not count holomorphic representatives, prove moduli regularity, or identify absolute gradings or an analytic invariant.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The actual flat grid, rectangle or consecutive row/column annulus, and the generator points and product end frames stated above.

[F1] The quotient determinant line has its Vandermonde ramification factor at every collision. In particular, for the constant nonzero tangent vector $V$ on $T$, the square of the wedge of its coordinate vectors descends to a section of $(\det TX)^2$; an isolated simple exchange of two roots gives one positive zero of this section. ([[lem-symmetric-product-quotient-determinant-has-vandermonde-ramification]])

[F2] Every continuous Whitney class has an actual smooth fixed-end model. Its index is the squared determinant boundary-phase winding with the specified product caps, is invariant under relative homotopy, and adds under concatenation; reversal negates it. ([[lem-continuous-whitney-classes-admit-relative-smooth-fixed-end-models]], [[lem-smooth-relative-whitney-homotopies-preserve-strip-fredholm-index]], [[lem-relative-strip-maslov-determinant-excision-and-local-models]])

[F3] For a smooth one-torus disk the boundary Maslov phase is the winding of its squared real tangent determinant in a complex disk frame; its compact real Fredholm index is $n$ plus that winding. This phase statement does not require the map to be a nonlinear holomorphic zero. ([[lem-geometric-oriented-disk-cauchy-riemann-fredholm-and-higher-regularity]])

[F4] Grid states have one point on each alpha and each beta circle, and rectangle orientation from $x$ to $y$ places $x$ northeast/southwest. ([[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]])

## Proof

1.1 Lift $R$ to the plane and write it as $c+[-a,a]+i[-b,b]$ with $a,b>0$ and side lengths less than $n$. Quotient this rectangle by $z\mapsto-z$ and use $w=z^2$ as its actual interior complex coordinate. This quotient is a disk: each radial ray in the $w$ plane has an interval from zero to its boundary, whose radial length is the square of the rectangle's radial length at half the angle. Its boundary consists of two arcs meeting at the two images of opposite corners; the map is smooth up to these arcs and their corners. Define the active roots to be $c+z,c-z$ modulo the torus periods and retain all inactive coordinates of $x$. The symmetric map is smooth at $w=0$ because its two active elementary symmetric coordinates are $2c,c^2-w$. Along the horizontal boundary arc the two roots lie on their original alpha circles; along the vertical arc they lie on their beta circles. Positive source-boundary orientation traverses the horizontal arc from the northeast/southwest tuple $x$ to the northwest/southeast tuple $y$. This constructs the stated continuous Whitney disk. [F4, given, construct, algebra]

1.2 Now let the row annulus be $i\le\operatorname{Im}z\le i+1$ modulo $n$, and put $c_y=i+1/2$ and $r=e^{-\pi/n}$. On $A=\{r\le|\zeta|\le r^{-1}\}$ define $$f(\zeta)=c_x+ic_y+\frac{n}{2\pi i}\log\zeta\pmod{n\mathbb Z+in\mathbb Z}.$$ Changing a logarithm adds $n$, so this is well defined and is a biholomorphism of the annulus interior onto the open row annulus. The map $p(\zeta)=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$ has the two simple branch points $\pm1$ and maps $A$ properly with degree two onto the closed ellipse with semiaxes $r+r^{-1}$ and $r^{-1}-r$. Indeed both boundary circles have that same ellipse as image, with reciprocal boundary points paired, and every fiber solves $\zeta^2-p\zeta+1=0$; the pair above $p=0$ lies inside $A$, so the two-root count is constant throughout the ellipse interior. No interior root can escape across its boundary without its image reaching that ellipse. The exterior contains no fiber in $A$, since the count is zero near infinity and its only possible crossing locus is the ellipse. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Its coordinate incidence surface is precisely the lifted rectangle, with one root above every generic point of its interior and none above its exterior; the inactive roots contribute constant maps only. Thus its point-divisor degrees are exactly the region chain $R$. No inactive root meets the rectangle: none lies on its boundary by the one-point-per-row/column condition, and none lies inside by the empty-state-interior hypothesis. Hence its only repeated tuple is the active exchange at $w=0$. In a local determinant frame the squared wedge section $\sigma$ from $V=1$ is a nonzero constant times $w$ there, by [F1]; it has no other zero. It follows that the boundary winding of $\sigma$ in any complex disk frame is $1$. This last equality is the finite argument principle for a line section: remove a small disk about its one zero, trivialize on finitely many patches of the remaining annulus, and cancel their common-edge argument changes, leaving the local winding $1$. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

2.2 Send this ellipse to a round disk by its positive diagonal real affine map. To each point of that disk assign the unordered pair of values $f(\zeta),f(\zeta^{-1})$ above it, and keep the remaining $n-2$ coordinates of $x$ fixed. It is an actual smooth symmetric map, including at the two branch points: in local coordinates its roots are exchanged by a holomorphic involution, and their elementary symmetric coefficients are holomorphic functions of $p$ before the real affine change. On the boundary one root lies on each of the two consecutive alpha circles. If the two required generator coordinates on the upper and lower circles have real lifts $x_u,x_l$, choose $c_x=(x_u+x_l)/2$ and $\theta=\pi(x_u-x_l)/n$. The boundary pair $\zeta=r e^{i\theta},\zeta^{-1}=r^{-1}e^{-i\theta}$ then gives exactly these generator entries. Taking its image point as the marked disk node makes this an actual based disk at $x$. The other roots lie on different alpha circles, hence outside the closed row annulus. The incidence map $f$ has degree one over that annulus and zero elsewhere, so its domain is the asserted unit annulus. [step 1.2, construct, algebra]

3.1 Relate this section to the actual strip caps, rather than identifying it with a compact disk problem with a single boundary condition. On the alpha boundary, the normalized squared determinant of the physical plane equals that of $\sigma$. On the beta boundary it equals $(-1)^n$ times that value, because each real coordinate vector is replaced by $iV$. At each marked corner all roots are distinct. Use its ordered flat product frame and the cap $e^{i\pi t/2}\mathbb R^n$, $0\le t\le1$. Its squared determinant is $e^{in\pi t}$ times the alpha value. Choose a continuous scalar function $t$ on the disk core, equal to $0$ on the alpha arc, $1$ on the beta arc, and to the indicated cap parameter on the two inserted constant corner collars. Such a function is obtained by interpolation in a rectangle model of the punctured disk; the collars are disjoint. Consequently the completed physical phase is the boundary phase of $\sigma$ multiplied by $e^{in\pi t}$. The second factor extends over the core, so has winding zero. The first has winding $1$ by step 2.1. Corner flattening in the two product charts by a real scalar cutoff preserves both planes, and changes this calculation only by a relative homotopy. [F2] therefore gives actual fixed-end index $1$, also for every allowed homotopic target complex structure. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 There are no coincidences with inactive coordinates. Equality of the two active values of $f$ would force their logarithmic arguments to differ by a torus period; their imaginary coordinates lie in an interval of length $1<n$, so only the horizontal period can occur. Therefore $\zeta^2=1$, precisely the two branch points. Since $df$ is nonzero there, [F1]'s section $\sigma$ has one positive simple zero at each, and no others. On the entire physical boundary its normalized value is the squared real tangent determinant for $L_\alpha$, since $V=1$ is tangent to every alpha circle. The finite line-section argument of step 2.1 and [F3] give boundary Maslov index $2$. A column annulus is obtained by the orientation-preserving torus rotation $z\mapsto iz$ from the same construction with the corresponding generator. Now $V=i$ is tangent to every beta circle; the constant factor $i^n$ in its wedge has no winding, so its boundary Maslov index is again $2$. This rotation is used only for a one-system based disk and does not exchange the alpha/beta conditions in the rectangle assertion. [F1, F3, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 2.2, construct, algebra]

4.1 Flatten either based disk near its node in a product chart by a real scalar cutoff, which preserves its one real boundary plane. Insert this disk on the corresponding side of the constant strip at $x$: glue its constant node collar to a small constant boundary interval of that strip, retaining both outer marked strip ends. A smooth rounded planar source for this glued disk is obtained by connecting their two collar rectangles and rounding their finitely many corners; both maps are constant on the joining rectangles. It is a continuous Whitney representative; the relative smoothing and fixed-end construction in [F2] supplies an actual smooth model. The completed determinant phase of its boundary is the constant strip's completed phase with the based disk's physical boundary phase inserted. The two joining constant intervals have identical frames, and their argument changes cancel; hence its winding is $0+2=2$. This directly proves its actual strip index without subtracting a compact disk's $n$-dimensional constant kernel. Domain degrees add by local winding and the inserted disk has its computed unit annulus domain. Finally [F2]'s actual class concatenation and reversal give all the stated sums and negative domains. No nonlinear holomorphic count or moduli regularity entered any step. [F2, F3, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $G'$ be an $X$ stabilization of type southwest of a knot grid $G$. In the four cells incident to the new crossing $c$, the northwest cell contains $X_1$, the northeast cell contains the new $O_1$, the southeast cell contains $X_2$, and the southwest cell is empty. Let $O_2$ be the old $O$ in the row of $X_2$. Write $I$ for states containing $c$, and identify such a state $\mathbf y$ with $e(\mathbf y)=\mathbf y\setminus\{c\}$ in $G$. Retain the independent variables of all markings.

An incoming left domain is either the zero domain or a nonnegative domain from $\mathbf x$ to $\mathbf y\in I$ with the following properties. At every state corner other than $c$, at least three adjacent cell multiplicities vanish; near $c$, three multiplicities equal $k$ and the southwest multiplicity is $k-1$; exactly $2k+1$ coordinates of $\mathbf y$ are absent from $\mathbf x$. For an incoming right domain, replace the southwest exception by southeast multiplicity $k+1$, and the number of absent coordinates by $2k+2$; the zero domain is not of right type. Denote these sets by $\pi^{iL},\pi^{iR}$. Define $D^{iL},D^{iR}$ by counting their targets $e(\mathbf y)$, with weight $\prod_{j\ne1}U_j^{O_j(p)}$, omitting the power of the new variable. Then
$$D=(D^{iL},D^{iR}):C^-(G')\longrightarrow\operatorname{Cone}(U_1+U_2:C^-(G)[U_1]\to C^-(G)[U_1])$$
is a finite polynomial-module chain map preserving Maslov degree and not increasing Alexander filtration. The first cone summand is shifted down by one in both degree and filtration. Its associated-graded map counts only domains avoiding $X_1,X_3,\ldots$; these have complexity at most two and give exactly the usual graded destabilization map: deletion of $c$ on $I$ in the first component, and rectangles through $X_2$ on the other states in the second component.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[alg-grid-knot-floer-complex]]

[[lem-grid-alexander-grading-integral]]

[[lem-grid-rectangle-boundary-square-zero-and-filtration]]

[[lem-grid-rectangle-differential-squares-to-zero]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, §13.3.2](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stabilized grid, marking labels, domain multiplicity conditions, and weighted map in the statement. The complexity of a nonzero incoming domain is the number of horizontal segments of its boundary; the zero domain has complexity one.

[F1] [[lem-grid-alexander-grading-integral]] supplies both rectangle grading formulas.

[F2] [[lem-grid-rectangle-boundary-square-zero-and-filtration]] supplies the two decompositions of nonreturning empty rectangle pairs and their equal monomial weights.

[F3] [[lem-grid-rectangle-differential-squares-to-zero]] proves the rectangle differentials square to zero.

## Proof

1.1 Follow the alternating horizontal and vertical boundary segments of an incoming domain, starting at the component of $\mathbf x$ on the new vertical circle. At an ordinary corner, three zero adjacent coefficients force the next segment and its direction; there is no choice to add an annulus without violating this condition at a state corner. The first segment and the distinguished vertical circle cut off a unique empty rectangle. Removing it gives the next boundary segment; remove the next forced rectangle as well. These two removals reduce the complexity by two and the three common local multiplicities at $c$ by one. Continuing ends at the zero domain for left type or the southeast rectangle for right type. This proves by induction a factorization into $m-1$ empty rectangles for complexity $m$, unique among factorizations in which every rectangle has a side on the new vertical circle. It also proves that left type has odd complexity $2k+1$ and right type even complexity $2k+2$. Both are bounded by the number of state coordinates. Since the set of empty rectangles is finite, only finitely many such factorizations and incoming domains occur. [given, construct]

1.2 Let $d'$ be the differential of $G'$ and $d$ that of $G$. To compare $D d'$ with the cone differential followed by $D$, lift rectangles of $G$ to $G'$ using the deletion correspondence. There are five possible rectangle types: A avoids $c$ and is empty; B has $c$ at a corner and is empty; C has $c$ in the interior of a side and is empty; D contains the initial-state point $c$ in its interior and no other state point; E contains $c$ in its interior while its initial state does not contain $c$, and is empty. Rectangles in $G$ correspond to types A and D. Rectangles counted in $d'$ have types A, B, C, E. In the cone there are also invisible terms, from its first to second copy, with coefficient $U_1+U_2$. [given, construct]

2.1 Apply [F1] to these $m-1$ rectangles. For a domain $p$ ending at $\mathbf y$, omission of the $U_1$ power gives the changes $A(\mathbf x)-A(U^{O_{\ne1}(p)}\mathbf y)=n_X(p)-O_1(p)$ and $M(\mathbf x)-M(U^{O_{\ne1}(p)}\mathbf y)=m-1-2O_1(p)$. For left type, $O_1(p)=k$ and $X_2(p)=k$; for right type, $O_1(p)=k$ and $X_2(p)=k+1$. Deleting $c$ raises the degree and Alexander value of a state in $I$ by one: in the finite pair-count formula, the new state corner contributes a loss of one in $M_O$ and none in $M_X$, so the Alexander loss is one as well. Account also for the downward shift in the first cone summand. The weighted output then has the same Maslov degree as its input, and its filtration drop is exactly $X_1(p)+X_3(p)+\cdots$, a nonnegative integer. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Classify a composition of an incoming domain of complexity $m$ and a rectangle by the rectangle type and number of common moving corners. The possible types are (A-0), (A-1), (A-2), (A-3); (B-0), (B-3), (B-4); (C-1); (D-0), (D-1); and the invisible type I. Here (B-0) has $m=1$, (B-3) has $m=3$, (B-4) has $m=2$; (A-2) requires $m\ge4$, (A-3) requires $m\ge3$, and (C-1),(D-1) require $m\ge2$. These are exhaustive: at an ordinary corner the three zero coefficients force the outgoing rectangle edge; counting its endpoints leaves precisely the listed numbers of common corners. A rectangle of type E cannot be followed by an incoming domain: following the latter's forced boundary from the new vertical circle would put either an initial-state point inside that rectangle or a terminal-state point in the incoming domain. The only extra edge in a type-D composition is the state point $c$, giving (D-0) or (D-1). [step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 Among (A-3) compositions, those wrapping through the horizontal row of $O_2$ are exceptional; those wrapping vertically through $O_1$ or horizontally through the row of $O_1$ are ordinary. Among (C-1) compositions, the exceptional case is a preceding rectangle containing both $X_1,O_1$ and an incoming domain of even complexity; the other two cases contain $X_1$ alone, or contain $X_2$ alone with odd complexity. Among (D-1) compositions, wrapping through the row of $O_2$ is exceptional; wrapping through $O_1$ is ordinary. Let $\delta$ be the incoming domain's innermost height for the cases involving $X_2$ or both $X_1,O_1$, and its innermost width for the case containing $X_1$ alone. Thus $\delta$ is a positive number of row or column strips. This specifies all subcases without imposing an $X$ exclusion. [step 2.2, construct]

3.2 Contributions of (A-0) cancel by commuting their disjoint boundary changes. Contributions of (A-1) cancel by cutting at the unique ordinary reflex corner in its two directions. The two resulting domain decompositions have the same total multiplicities, hence the same monomial. An (A-2) composition of incoming complexity $m+2$ cancels with (D-0) of complexity $m>1$: slide the cut through the two consecutive boundary segments next to $c$, thereby moving the state point $c$ from a counted incoming domain into the lifted rectangle's interior. The same slide for (D-0) of complexity one yields (B-3) of complexity three. These are inverse cut operations, so every contribution in these classes appears once in its indicated pair. [F2, step 1.1, step 2.2, construct]

4.1 The two (B-4) domains are the vertical thin annulus through $O_1,X_2$ and horizontal thin annulus through $O_2,X_2$. Their weights are respectively $U_1$ and $U_2$, since in this case the rectangle, rather than the incoming domain, carries that variable. Their sum cancels the invisible term applied to the zero incoming domain. A (B-0) rectangle ending at $c$ cancels with an ordinary (A-3) composition of complexity three: adjoin the row or column annulus through $O_1$ according as $c$ is the rectangle's upper-left or lower-right corner, and cut at the other two corners. This operation inserts two extra boundary segments and reverses when that annulus is removed. The added $O_1$ multiplicity lies in the incoming part, whose weight omits $U_1$, so the coefficients agree. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

4.2 For an ordinary (C-1) composition $r*p$ containing $X_2$, adjoin the horizontal thin annulus through $O_1$; for the case containing $X_1$ alone, adjoin the vertical thin annulus through $O_1$. If $\delta=1$, the forced alternative cut is (D-1) of the same incoming complexity; if $\delta>1$, it is ordinary (A-3) with complexity greater by two. In both cases the alternative domain has exactly one contributing cut: its location is forced by the first state point in the added strip. Removing the strip recovers $r*p$, so these cancellations are bijections. Again the added annulus changes only the omitted $O_1$ exponent in the incoming part. Therefore each pair has equal coefficient. [step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 For an exceptional (C-1) composition of even complexity $2k$, the composite itself is an incoming left domain of complexity $2k+1$ and gives an invisible contribution. Adjoin the horizontal thin annulus through $O_2$ and use the forced alternative cut. If $\delta=1$, that cut has type exceptional (D-1) and complexity $2k$; if $\delta>1$, it has type exceptional (A-3) and complexity $2k+2$. The (C-1) rectangle contributes an additional $U_1$ because it contains $O_1$; the annulus-added alternative contributes an additional $U_2$; the invisible term contributes $U_1+U_2$. The remaining monomial is common to all three, so their total vanishes. Removing the added strip or viewing the invisible incoming domain with its first cut recovers the same triple, with no duplication. This exhausts exceptional (D-1), exceptional (A-3) and invisible terms of complexity greater than one. Together with the preceding cancellation cases, every term in $D d'+d_{\mathrm{cone}}D$ has cancelled. Thus $D$ is a chain map. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 4.2, algebra]

6.1 By step 2.1, the associated-graded map retains just domains avoiding $X_1,X_3,\ldots$. The northwest cell contains $X_1$ and has local multiplicity $k$ in either nontrivial type. Avoiding $X_1$ therefore forces $k=0$. Left type would then have southwest multiplicity $-1$, so its only surviving term is the separately allowed zero domain. ## Statement

Assume countable choice. In a nonempty generic marked rectangular diagram call a horizontal segment a cap if its two incident vertical segments extend to the same side in height, and monotone otherwise. A generalized bridge rectification has three kinds of horizontal segment: an empty cap, a monotone segment with exactly one crossing, and an empty monotone segment, called a regular jog. Smooth the first two kinds as in a bridge-like grid and tilt and round each regular jog monotonically in height. This produces a bridge diagram with one distinguished regular point for each jog, at pairwise distinct heights different from all critical and crossing heights. For a jog remember also whether its lower incident vertical piece is to the left or to the right of its upper incident piece. This is its side datum.

Two generalized bridge rectifications whose smoothed diagrams with distinguished points are bridge isotopic, with the same side data, are connected by finitely many disjoint-interval column commutations after normalization of coordinate orders. Every generalized bridge rectification is related by finite grid stabilizations, legal commutations and destabilizations to an ordinary bridge-like grid whose smoothing has the same bridge-isotopy class after forgetting the distinguished regular points.

More explicitly, a vertical grid piece in column $P$ from a mark $a$ at lower row $L$ to its complementary mark at upper row $T$ may be split at any regular height $L<h<T$. Insert $Q$ immediately right of $P$ and $J$ immediately above $L$, replace $(P,L,a)$ by $(P,J,a),(Q,J,\bar a),(Q,L,a)$, and commute the short row $J$ to the gap containing $h$. Here $\bar a$ is the other marking type. This inserts a crossing-free jog with the lower piece on the right. Insertion to the left gives the other side. These constructions, their inverses, and the preceding uniqueness assertion do not use global grid-isotopy generation.

A legal commutation exchanges adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. A stabilization replaces a marking by a three-mark two-by-two block with its type twice at opposite corners, the complementary type once, and one empty corner, preserving one of each type per row and column.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite oriented generalized bridge diagrams, their distinguished jog points and side data, and the explicit grid-move conventions in the statement.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] fixes the row $O$-to-$X$, column $X$-to-$O$, and vertical-over conventions.

[F2] [[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]] supplies an ordinary bridge-like grid for every nonempty bridge diagram, and commutation equivalence for ordinary rectifications with bridge-isotopic smoothings.

## Proof

1.1 Associate pieces to a jog-marked bridge diagram by cutting at extrema, undercrossing preimages and the distinguished regular points, leaving each overcrossing branch uncut. Every resulting piece is strictly height-monotone and has a nondegenerate closed height interval. At a critical or crossing height use its ordinary local cap or crossing order. At a distinguished regular height its two incident pieces lie consecutively among the local vertical pieces; prescribe their order by the side datum. This prescription is consistent with all other pieces: the distinguished point has a small disk disjoint from every other branch, and both incident vertical positions can be placed arbitrarily close to its original position on the selected sides. Pieces whose closed height intervals overlap have one prescribed left-to-right inequality, given by the graph order on an interior regular height or by this endpoint prescription. For every set of intervals containing a common height, these inequalities give a coherent total order. [given, construct]

2.1 The inequalities have no directed cycle. Three pairwise intersecting closed intervals have a common point, by comparing their largest left endpoint with their smallest right endpoint, so a triangle has coherent order. An interval intersection graph has no chordless cycle of length at least four: at a vertex with largest left endpoint both neighbors contain that endpoint and hence intersect each other. A chord of a shortest directed cycle, in either direction, would shorten it. Thus there is no directed cycle. Repeated removal of a vertex with no incoming edge gives a total order extending all inequalities, and assigning distinct increasing coordinates realizes them. At a critical height its horizontal join is an empty cap; at a crossing height the join meets exactly the overpassing piece; at a jog height its incident endpoints are consecutive and its join is empty and monotone. This constructs generalized rectifications with the stipulated incidence and side data. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 The coordinate solution set is the open convex set defined by those strict inequalities. The special and distinguished height order is fixed in a bridge isotopy; pieces and their local orders continue without alteration. Hence two generalized rectifications of the same marked bridge class give two points of this same convex set after identifying pieces. Join them by a piecewise linear path which crosses each coordinate-equality hyperplane transversely and one at a time: choose an intermediate point in a small open ball avoiding the finitely many affine hyperplanes that force parallel or simultaneous crossings. Finitely many proper affine hyperplanes cannot cover an open ball, as their defining polynomial product is nonzero on some line segment. Only pieces with disjoint closed height intervals can meet in coordinate along this path, since intersecting intervals have a fixed strict inequality. At such a meeting the two columns are adjacent. The normalized grids therefore differ by a finite sequence of disjoint-interval column commutations. Ordered changes of height coordinates alter no normalized grid. This proves the uniqueness assertion, including closed interval endpoints at the distinguished heights. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

3.2 We also verify the bridge interpretation used here. On each interval of regular heights all pieces are ordered graphs, so ordered rectangular replacements have the same graph order. At a jog the replacement can be smoothed as a strictly height-monotone arc, with the same unique graph on each nearby horizontal fiber. At a crossing the difference of the two graph abscissae has a simple zero, so the positive affine horizontal map matching the two graph values extends smoothly over that zero by division by their simple vanishing factor. At a cap choose the small central smoothing as an affine horizontal image of the original Morse cap, and connect to its vertical legs by monotone branches in an empty neighborhood. Between these finitely many special neighborhoods extend the prescribed horizontal maps by positive derivatives on each gap: choose short end collars matching the prescribed derivatives, then a nonnegative interior bump whose integral fills the required positive image gap. Compact regular subbands give positive separation bounds. Smooth partitions in the height coordinate patch these maps by convex combinations, preserving positive horizontal derivative and all matching values. Outside a large rectangle take the identity. Interpolating the resulting increasing horizontal fiber maps with the identity, and separately interpolating increasing height reparameterizations, gives plane diffeomorphisms throughout. They prove the required bridge isotopies. The regular-jog case adds no singularity or critical point to this construction. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 The stated insertion is an actual marked stabilization. With $J>L$ and $Q>P$, the new block has $a$ northwest and southeast, $\bar a$ northeast and empty southwest. Row $L$ keeps its exterior $\bar a$, column $P$ keeps its exterior $\bar a$ at $T$, and the new row and column have one marking of each type. The new row interval is $[P,Q]$. Since these columns are adjacent, each old intervening row between $L,T$ has its endpoints outside that interval: its endpoints cannot be on $P$ except in rows $L,T$, and cannot be on the new $Q$. It is thus disjoint from $[P,Q]$ or strictly contains it. Commute $J$ upward one neighboring row at a time to the desired gap. No swap with $L,T$ is needed. Every exchange is legal. In that gap the new horizontal segment has one incident vertical leg above and one below, and crosses no old column, so it is a regular jog. Old crossing and critical height orders are unchanged. Its smoothing is bridge isotopic to the original after forgetting the distinguished point, by the local monotone-graph construction of step 3.2. [F1, given, construct, cases]

5.1 If the lower incident piece is to be on the left, insert $Q$ immediately left of $P$ instead. Use the same marks $(P,J,a),(Q,J,\bar a),(Q,L,a)$ and remove $(P,L,a)$. The new block now has $\bar a$ northwest, $a$ northeast and southwest, and empty southeast; it is again an allowed stabilization. The same adjacent-column interval argument moves the new row to the chosen height. Reflection here specifies a second finite recipe; no move from a grid to its reflection is assumed. Either type $a$ works by [F1]. Repeating these finite constructions inserts any finite ordered list of regular jogs and side data on the monotone pieces of an ordinary bridge rectification. An already inserted jog merely subdivides a piece; the next chosen regular point lies in one of its still vertical subpieces, to which the same construction applies. [F1, step 4.1, construct, cases]

6.1 Finally take a generalized bridge rectification $G$ and let $D$ be its jog-marked smoothing. Forget the regular points and choose an ordinary bridge rectification $B$ by [F2]. The distinguished points of $D$ lie on its monotone pieces at heights different from all special heights, so the two insertion recipes insert their matching ordered points and side data into $B$, giving a generalized grid $B'$. Steps 1.1–3.2 identify $B'$ and $G$ by disjoint-interval column commutations. Reverse those insertions to obtain a finite grid-move sequence from $G$ to $B$. This is an explicit reduction through fixed marked bridge data, not an appeal to planar invariance of an unproved global assignment. It proves every assertion. [F2, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let a smooth planar isotopy have exactly one exceptional bridge time in a small parameter interval. At that time two spatially distinct special points have equal height and exchange height order transversely. Each is a nondegenerate height maximum, a nondegenerate height minimum, or a transverse crossing with neither branch height-critical. All other special heights are distinct and different from this common height, no other bridge degeneracy occurs, and the diagrams on either side are nonempty bridge diagrams. Then there are bridge-like grid rectifications on the two sides with identical column order and all but two row orders identical. The remaining adjacent rows have disjoint closed marking intervals and exchange by one legal row commutation, meaning the exchange of two adjacent rows whose closed horizontal marking intervals are disjoint or strictly nested. The oriented markings and crossing decorations are transported unchanged. All other choices of rectification on either side are connected to these by commutations.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The planar isotopy and isolated special-height exchange specified in the statement.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] fixes the grid marking and vertical-over convention.

[F2] [[lem-bridge-diagram-grid-rectification]] constructs bridge-like rectifications from the finite ordered height data and identifies all rectifications of one bridge-isotopy class by commutations.

## Proof

1.1 Denote the exceptional points at the exceptional time by $p,q$ and their common height by $c$. Since they are distinct points of that horizontal line, their abscissae are distinct. Choose disjoint small disks around them with disjoint horizontal projections, avoiding every other crossing or critical point. In a thin horizontal band about $c$, all branches outside these disks are height-monotone. Such a band exists: otherwise critical points outside the disks would converge to height $c$, contrary to the hypotheses and compactness. Shrink the parameter interval so the two designated event neighborhoods remain disjoint with the same horizontal order, and no other special height enters this band. The two designated heights are adjacent in the full special-height order on either side. [given, construct]

2.1 Cut the diagram at all extrema and all undercrossing preimages, keeping an overcrossing branch uncut, as in [F2]. Away from the two designated points the resulting height-monotone pieces continue uniquely across the event. No one such piece can have two distinct preimages at the common height $c$ in the exceptional diagram. On its interior the height derivative is nonzero with constant sign, so its height is strictly monotone; allowing an extremum or undercrossing endpoint does not change strict monotonicity between distinct points. In particular a piece cannot join the two spatially distinct designated points or pass through one while ending at the other. Thus their local endpoint and crossing configurations involve no identification that would force the same vertical piece into both event disks at height $c$. [F2, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 Form closed height intervals for all these pieces at the exceptional diagram, allowing the two local joins at the same height $c$. Prescribe left-to-right inequalities whenever two intervals intersect, using the regular height order in the interior and the local cap or crossing order at an endpoint. At height $c$, place the entire local endpoint/crossing group at $p$ before the group at $q$ if $p$ is left of $q$, and conversely if $q$ is left. This order is compatible with every other piece, since its abscissa at height $c$ avoids the two disjoint disks; pieces inside a single disk have precisely the ordinary cap or crossing order. Step 2.1 excludes duplicated pieces within those two groups. Consequently every set of intervals containing one common height has a coherent total order, even at $c$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 These inequalities have a solution in distinct abscissae. To give the finite argument, any triangle of intersecting intervals has a common point, since their largest left endpoint does not exceed their smallest right endpoint. It therefore has no directed cycle by step 3.1. In any cycle of length at least four in an interval intersection graph, choose the vertex with largest left endpoint. Both neighbors contain that endpoint and hence have a chord between them. Either orientation of this chord shortens a directed cycle. Thus there is no directed cycle of inequalities. Repeatedly remove a vertex without an incoming edge and assign increasing distinct integers in that order. This solves every inequality. In particular the horizontal join intervals at $p,q$ are disjoint, including their endpoints: all of one join's endpoints precede all of the other's, by their disjoint local groups in step 3.1. Their overpassing vertical segments, if present, lie within their own join intervals, not between the two groups. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Keep these abscissae fixed, and replace the two equal special heights by two nearby distinct heights in either order. The resulting vertical/horizontal picture is valid in both orders. One way to check that no constraint was missed is to enlarge every interval endpoint originally at $c$ slightly before separating the two levels. All new overlaps occur among pieces whose old intervals contained $c$, hence already have the coherent order of step 3.1. Every other overlap is unchanged if the separation is sufficiently small, since there are finitely many endpoint levels separated from $c$. A cap still has no vertical piece between its endpoints at its level, and a crossing join still has exactly its designated overpassing piece there; the only other local join lies in the disjoint abscissa group. Thus each picture is a bridge-like rectangular diagram with the original oriented incidence and vertical-over crossing data. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 The ordered graph and local special-point data of these two pictures agree with the given isotopy just before and just after the exchange. The fiberwise bridge-isotopy construction of [F2], applied on each side where the special heights are distinct, identifies their smoothings with those diagrams. Both normalized grids have the same column order. Their row orders differ solely by exchanging the two designated adjacent levels, whose horizontal marking intervals are disjoint by step 4.1. This is exactly a legal row commutation by [F1]. The same corner incidence and oriented traversal give the same $O,X$ labels before and after; the exchange does not redecorate any crossing. Finally [F2] connects any other rectifications on either side to the constructed ones by commutations. The proof did not distinguish maximum, minimum and crossing beyond their proved local join orders, so every pair of the stated special-point types, with every orientation and crossing decoration, is included. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Use planar grid markings with horizontal orientation $O$ to $X$, vertical
orientation $X$ to $O$, and vertical segments over horizontal segments.
Allowed commutations exchange adjacent rows or columns whose closed marking
intervals are disjoint or one is contained in the interior of the other.
Stabilizations split a row and a column at a chosen marking into a
three-mark $2\times2$ block, with the chosen type twice, the other type once,
and one empty corner; every new row and column has one of each type.
Destabilizations are their inverses. A row exchange with a shared marking
column is not assumed to be an allowed commutation.

Suppose a finite grid has four consecutive columns $L,B,M,R$ and two
consecutive rows $H<K$. For $a\in\{O,X\}$, with $\bar a$ the opposite type,
its markings on those rows are exactly
$$H:\ (L,a),(M,\bar a),\qquad K:\ (M,a),(R,\bar a).$$
The other markings of $L,R$ lie below $H$. Column $B$ has its markings in
rows $D<H$ and $T>K$, in either orientation. Thus the capped strand runs
through the two horizontal segments $L$ to $M$ and $M$ to $R$, and is
underpassing at its crossing with $B$.

Four allowed grid moves produce a grid whose active column order is
$L,M,B,R$ and whose active rows have markings
$$H:\ (M,a),(R,\bar a),\qquad K:\ (L,a),(M,\bar a).$$
Its other markings are exactly those obtained by first exchanging columns
$B,M$ and then exchanging the contents of rows $H,K$. The latter
shared-endpoint row exchange is realized by a stabilization, one allowed
commutation, and a destabilization, rather than used as a primitive move.

More explicitly, first commute $B,M$. Insert a column $V$ immediately
right of $L$, between $L,M$, and a row $J$ between $H,K$, by stabilizing
at $(L,H)$. Then commute $J,K$ and destabilize the block in columns
$V,M$ and rows $H,K$. Delete the old column $M$ and old row $K$,
and rename $V$ as $M$ and $J$ as $K$. The complete certificate is:

| Stage | Active column order | Active row order | Marked rows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | $L,B,M,R$ | $H<K$ | $H:(L,a),(M,\bar a)$; $K:(M,a),(R,\bar a)$ |
| 1 | $L,M,B,R$ | $H<K$ | Same labeled markings |
| 2 | $L,V,M,B,R$ | $H<J<K$ | $H:(V,a),(M,\bar a)$; $J:(L,a),(V,\bar a)$; $K:(M,a),(R,\bar a)$ |
| 3 | $L,V,M,B,R$ | $H<K<J$ | Same labeled markings as stage 2 |
| 4 | $L,M,B,R$ | $H<K$ | $H:(M,a),(R,\bar a)$; $K:(L,a),(M,\bar a)$ |

Initially $B$ crosses the lower segment on the left side of the capped
strand; finally it crosses the lower segment on its right side, and remains
overpassing. Both choices of $a$ and both orientations of $B$ are covered.
Reflecting the entire certificate in either coordinate axis supplies the
opposite-side and minimum versions without exchanging horizontal and
vertical segments or changing the overpassing convention.

This is a conditional local certificate with the stated adjacency and
partner-height hypotheses. Bringing arbitrary bridge approximations into
this form, and global grid-move generation, are separate assertions.

## Statement references

[[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]]

[Ozsvath, Stipsicz and Szabo, *Grid Homology for Knots and Links*, Exercise3.1.11 and AppendixB.4](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~petero/GridHomologyBook.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite grid and its consecutive active columns, consecutive active rows, marked corners, and exterior-partner heights specified in the statement.

[F1] [[def-grid-diagram-for-an-oriented-knot]] supplies one marking of each type per row and column, horizontal orientation $O$ to $X$, vertical orientation $X$ to $O$, and vertical-over crossing data.

## Proof

1.1 In column $M$ the two markings lie at $H,K$. The interval $[H,K]$ lies strictly inside the interval $[D,T]$ of $B$, because $D<H<K<T$. Columns $B,M$ are adjacent. Their exchange is therefore an allowed nested-interval commutation, giving stage 1. It carries the whole column, including both exterior markings of $B$, and makes $L,M$ adjacent. No other mark changes its row. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 Stabilize the marking $a$ at $(L,H)$, inserting $V$ immediately right of $L$ and $J$ immediately above $H$. Put $a$ at $(L,J)$ and $(V,H)$, put $\bar a$ at $(V,J)$, and leave $(L,H)$ empty. Thus the new block has northwest $a$, northeast $\bar a$, southeast $a$, and empty southwest: it is an $a:\mathrm{SW}$ stabilization. The former other marking $(M,H)$ of row $H$ stays on that row, and the former other marking of column $L$ stays in that column. Row $H$ now has $(V,a),(M,\bar a)$; row $J$ has $(L,a),(V,\bar a)$; all columns and rows still contain one of each type. Row $K$ remains $(M,a),(R,\bar a)$. This proves stage 2 with column order $L<V<M<B<R$ and row order $H<J<K$. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Rows $J,K$ are adjacent. Their closed horizontal intervals are $[L,V]$ and $[M,R]$. Since $L<V<M<R$, these are disjoint, including their endpoints. Their exchange is an allowed commutation. It gives stage 3, with row order $H<K<J$ and the same labeled marking pairs. This exchange uses no shared-endpoint interval rule. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 At stage 3, columns $V,M$ are adjacent and rows $H,K$ are adjacent. In their block the northwest cell $(V,K)$ is empty; northeast $(M,K)$ and southwest $(V,H)$ have $a$; southeast $(M,H)$ has $\bar a$. The other marking of the two-row block is $\bar a$ at $(R,K)$, outside these two columns. The other marking of the two-column block is $\bar a$ at $(V,J)$, outside these two rows. This is an $a:\mathrm{NW}$ stabilization block in reverse. Contract it by deleting column $M$ and row $K$, retaining $a$ at the merged corner $(V,H)$, and moving the exterior block marking $(R,K)$ to $(R,H)$. The marking $(V,J)$ stays in column $V$. After renaming $V$ as $M$ and $J$ as $K$, the two rows are exactly $H:(M,a),(R,\bar a)$ and $K:(L,a),(M,\bar a)$. Each retains one $O$ and one $X$. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 The stabilization inserted $V$ between the adjacent columns $L,M$; deletion of the old $M$ makes $V$ occupy precisely that old column's rank. Similarly $J$ was inserted between the adjacent rows $H,K$, exchanged with $K$, and remains at the original $K$ rank after the old row $K$ is deleted. Therefore the three-move subcertificate changes no other row or column rank and realizes exactly the exchange of the two original row contents. Column $L$'s lower partner and column $R$'s lower partner stay fixed, while the only exterior displacement in the complete four-move certificate is the already specified exchange of columns $B,M$ in step 1.1. All untouched rows and columns retain their marking counts. This verifies the full exterior marking assertion, not merely the unmarked local arcs. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 In the initial column order $L<B<M<R$, column $B$ crosses the row-$H$ segment $[L,M]$, and lies outside the row-$K$ segment $[M,R]$. In the final order $L<M<B<R$, it crosses the row-$H$ segment $[M,R]$ and lies outside the row-$K$ segment $[L,M]$. Its interval still runs from below $H$ to above $K$, and it is over at both crossings by [F1]. The capped strand, whose exterior legs at $L,R$ end below $H$, is the underpassing height-critical branch in this pair of rectangular patterns. If $a=O$ it runs from the lower $L$ leg to the lower $R$ leg; $a=X$ reverses that direction. The types at every new corner were explicitly checked in steps 2.1 and 4.1, so either orientation of that strand and either choice of the two exterior types on $B$ works. Horizontal or vertical reflection preserves adjacency and strict containment or disjointness, and reflects each legal three-mark block to another legal stabilization block. Vertical segments remain vertical and overpassing. Thus the reflected opposite-side and minimum certificates are also valid; no equivalence from a grid to its own reflection and no axis-exchange shortcut is assumed. The four stated moves and all marking checks are finite, so no choice axiom is used. [F1, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $G$ be a knot grid of size $n\ge2$ on its actual flat torus, with horizontal alpha and vertical beta circles and the product-integrable end data. Let $u:x\to y$ be any REALIZED continuous Whitney class, with integral domain $D$. At a grid vertex $v$ write $\nu_v(D)$ for one quarter of the sum of its four adjacent cell coefficients, and put $n_x(D)=\sum_{v\in x}\nu_v(D)$. Then its actual fixed-end real index before translation is
$$\mu(u)=n_x(D)+n_y(D).$$
This includes signed domains and positive marked degrees. If every cell coefficient is nonnegative and $\mu(u)=1$, then $x,y$ differ in exactly two points and $D$ is exactly one embedded torus rectangle from $x$ to $y$, of multiplicity one and with no state point in its interior. No exclusion of $O$ or $X$ marks is imposed. Its row and column intervals are both proper cyclic intervals, so it is an ordinary rectangle among the four choices for those changed corners.

This proves actual index and domain classification, not existence or uniqueness of holomorphic representatives, their count, equality of equal-domain homotopy classes, or a grid-to-analytic chain equivalence.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The flat grid and actual class, with its usual region degrees and generator ends.

[F1] The full realized-grid grading theorem constructs for every realized domain an equal-domain actual concatenation of empty-state rectangles and signed unit row/column annulus loops. Their actual indices are one and two, respectively, and actual indices add and agree on equal domains. The same theorem gives $\mu=M_O(x)-M_O(y)+2\sum n_O$. ([[thm-realized-grid-whitney-classes-have-the-full-relative-grading-formula]], [[lem-grid-empty-rectangle-and-annulus-classes-have-explicit-indices]])

[F2] For arbitrary smooth Whitney models, ordered roots and compact Stokes identify domain jumps with the signed labelled coordinate boundary paths. The conclusion includes arbitrary signed local multiplicities, and smooth models represent all the continuous classes in [F1]. ([[lem-equal-whitney-domains-have-equal-boundary-windings-and-fredholm-index]])

[F3] Compact Stokes holds for finite smooth surface cells and smooth one-forms, without full Choice. ([[lem-finite-chart-localization-defines-choice-free-integration-and-compact-stokes]])

## Proof

1.1 Number cells by $(i,j)\in(\mathbb Z/n)^2$, with cell $D_{ij}$ northeast of vertex $(i,j)$. Define the vertex functions $$\Delta D_{ij}=D_{ij}+D_{i-1,j-1}-D_{i-1,j}-D_{i,j-1},\qquad QD_{ij}=\tfrac14(D_{ij}+D_{i-1,j-1}+D_{i-1,j}+D_{i,j-1}).$$ For the actual domain one has $\Delta D=1_x-1_y$. Here is the local boundary verification. By [F2], the jump across each open alpha edge counts its actual labelled boundary path with sign. At an alpha-beta crossing its change from the preceding to the succeeding edge is the endpoint coefficient of that path, namely one at its source state point and minus one at its target state point. The alternating four cell sum displayed above is exactly that change, with the grid orientation in which a rectangle has its source at southwest/northeast. Common state points cancel. Full-circle winding terms are constant on the circle and introduce no change. Equivalently apply [F2]'s ordered-root Stokes calculation on the four edges of a small crossing neighborhood; each labelled path appears with its actual degree, so division by the finite ordered-cover degree gives this same endpoint coefficient. Thus the assertion holds for signed degrees as well as positive ones. Also $QD=\nu(D)$ by definition. [F2, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 The finite pairing $\langle\Delta E,QD\rangle$ is symmetric in $D,E$. To check this without a boundary term, let $S_i,S_j$ be the backward cyclic shifts on cell arrays. Then $\Delta=(1-S_i)(1-S_j)$, $Q=(1+S_i)(1+S_j)/4$, and, for the ordinary finite sum pairing, $S_i^*=S_i^{-1}$ and $S_j^*=S_j^{-1}$. All shifts commute. Hence $$\Delta^*Q=\tfrac14(S_i-S_i^{-1})(S_j-S_j^{-1})$$ is self-adjoint: transposing changes the sign of each of its two factors. This proves the stated symmetry by a finite matrix identity, including cells crossing either chosen seam. No fundamental-square pair-count convention is needed here. [step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 For a domain $D:x\to y$ put $F_{xy}(D)=\langle1_x+1_y,QD\rangle$. If $E:y\to z$, step 1.1 and step 2.1 give $$F_{xz}(D+E)-F_{xy}(D)-F_{yz}(E)=\langle1_z-1_y,QD\rangle+\langle1_x-1_y,QE\rangle=-\langle\Delta E,QD\rangle+\langle\Delta D,QE\rangle=0.$$ It negates under endpoint reversal and domain negation. On an empty-state rectangle, its four changed corner measures are $1/4$ each, and all common state measures vanish, so $F=1$. On a unit row annulus loop, exactly two state points are on its bounding horizontal circles, each of measure $1/2$; all others have measure zero. Thus $F_{xx}=2n_x=2$. A column annulus has the same count on its two bounding vertical circles. For $n=2$ these two circles are still distinct and the same calculation applies. By [F1] concatenate these actual models to match $D$, using signs for negative annuli. Additivity makes $F_{xy}(D)$ equal their actual index sum; equal-domain index comparison in [F1] identifies this sum with $\mu(u)$. This proves the all-realized-class point-measure formula. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Assume now $D\ge0$ and $\mu=1$. If $x=y$, the last formula in [F1] makes its index the even integer $2\sum n_O$, impossible. Otherwise let $r$ be the number of points of $x$ not in $y$. The state-permutation condition gives $r\ge2$: changing exactly one point cannot preserve both its row and column. There are $2r$ changed vertices. At each, $|\Delta D|=1$ by step 1.1. Since its four coefficients are nonnegative integers, their sum is at least one, so its point measure is at least $1/4$. Common vertices have nonnegative measure and occur twice in $n_x+n_y$. Thus step 3.1 gives $1\ge r/2$, forcing $r=2$. Equality forces precisely one adjacent cell coefficient one and the other three zero at every changed vertex, and all four coefficients zero at every common vertex. In particular all changed corners are convex, with no reflex or higher-multiplicity alternative. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Only the two changed rows and two changed columns can support the chain boundary of $D$. On any other horizontal circle its jump is constant between crossings, by step 1.1, since there is no changed endpoint on that circle; at its common state point both adjacent coefficients vanish by step 4.1, so the jump is zero everywhere. The same holds for any other vertical circle. On each changed row, its two changed vertices divide it into two proper cyclic arcs. The jump is constant on each open arc; the one-positive-quadrant pattern at either endpoint says one arc has jump of magnitude one and the other zero. The same conclusion holds on each changed column. Thus the entire boundary consists of four oriented arcs connecting those four vertices, one on each changed circle, each of multiplicity one. They form one four-edge cycle: every vertex has one horizontal and one vertical incident arc and the rows and columns are distinct. Since this is the boundary of the actual torus cell chain, its integrals against the global closed forms $dx,dy$ vanish by [F3]. The two horizontal arcs therefore have opposite signed displacements of the same magnitude, so they select the same proper column interval in opposite directions. The vertical arcs likewise select the same proper row interval. Consequently this cycle is the boundary of the embedded product of those two intervals, a torus rectangle $R$. The positive-quadrant pattern fixes the boundary sign as $+\partial R$, rather than its negative: the latter would have three positive adjacent quadrants after adding a constant, not exactly one. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Now $\partial(D-R)=0$. Across each grid edge its two coefficients agree, so the connected rectangular torus grid makes $D-R$ a constant multiple of the whole torus. At a changed corner the three exterior coefficients of $D$ and of $R$ are all zero; hence that constant is zero and $D=R$. All common state point measures vanish by step 4.1, so no common point lies inside $R$. Its only remaining state points are its two source and two target corners. Finally $\Delta R=1_x-1_y$ fixes which alternating corners are the source; this is exactly the oriented rectangle convention. Marks were never restricted, and their positive degrees remain allowed. This completes only the stated index and positive-domain classification. [step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume full AC. For the smooth based unknot $U\subset S^3$, the integral singular earring instanton group is isomorphic to $\mathbb Z$, and its rationalization has dimension one. There are regular choices with one critical generator and zero differential. Its generator is specified only up to the usual orientation sign; no distinguished sign-independent canonical class or sutured-excision identification is asserted.

## Statement references

[[def-instanton-knot-homology-and-canonical-class]]

[Kronheimer–Mrowka, Proposition4.1](https://people.math.harvard.edu/~kronheim/khovanov-unknot.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] Actual earring singular models, the fixed-determinant exterior lift and central determinant-one stabilizers are supplied by [[lem-earring-relative-arc-data-supply-admissible-orbifold-and-determinant-lifts]].

[F2] The integral complex and independence of regular choices are the precise analytic interface of [[lem-instanton-knot-complex-asd-analytic-foundations]]. Its all-index perturbations may preserve every critical jet, and its actual loop indices are divisible by four. [[lem-earring-holonomy-perturbations-regularize-all-trajectory-indices]] [[lem-earring-gauge-components-force-index-energy-monotonicity]]

[F3] A compact circle isotopy in the boundaryless $S^3\setminus U$ extends to an ambient isotopy supported away from $U$ by [[thm-isotopy-extension]]. Full AC is inherited through [F1]–[F2]. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

## Proof

**Given:** The based unknot and its actual small meridional earring and relative arc class. The argument uses the declared analytic interface [F2], whose separate proof is not a surgery or KHI theorem.

1.1 **An explicit product exterior.** Write $S^3=\{(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2:|z_1|^2+|z_2|^2=1\}$ and take $U=\{z_2=0\}$. At $(1,0)$ its small normal meridian is $L_r=\{(\cos r,\sin r e^{i\theta})\}$ for a small $r>0$. Increasing $r$ to $\pi/2$ is a smooth isotopy of embedded circles disjoint from $U$; [F3] extends it while fixing $U$. The resulting earring is the other coordinate circle. Away from the two coordinate circles the map $(\theta_1,\theta_2,s)\mapsto(\cos s e^{i\theta_1},\sin s e^{i\theta_2})$, $0<s<\pi/2$, is an actual diffeomorphism. Removing small invariant coordinate tubes therefore gives $T^2\times[s_0,s_1]$. Its two meridians are the two circle coordinates. The relative arc has one endpoint on each boundary torus, so its dual $w_2$ evaluates one on a product torus, just as in [F1]. [F1, F3, given, construct, algebra]

2.1 **The twisted flat holonomies and the allowed gauge quotient.** A flat $SO(3)$ bundle on this exterior is described by its commuting meridian holonomies. On a flat product-torus square the obstruction to lifting its four edge identifications is the commutator of their $SU(2)$ lifts, so $w_2=1$ means $ab=-ba$. Both meridians have the prescribed half-turn adjoint holonomy. Their lifts are unit imaginary quaternions, and $ab+ba=-2\langle a,b\rangle$ makes their axes perpendicular. Conjugation is transitive on ordered perpendicular unit axes, so take $(a,b)=(i,j)$. Conversely the flat bundle formed from $\mathbb R^2\times[s_0,s_1]\times SO(3)$ with deck fiber maps $\operatorname{Ad}i,\operatorname{Ad}j$ realizes this data. Its two ends extend as the flat local earring models of [F1], so it gives a global singular flat connection. One must also check the determinant-one quotient, rather than silently using all $SO(3)$ gauges. The obstruction of an $SO(3)$ gauge to a determinant-one lift is its sign class on the two fundamental loops, in $H^1(T^2;\mathbb Z/2)$. The parallel adjoint gauges with values $\operatorname{Ad}i$ and $\operatorname{Ad}j$ have obstruction classes $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, respectively: their lifts commute with their own meridian lift and anticommute with the other. They span all four obstruction classes. Composing any full gauge comparison with such a parallel stabilizer kills its lifting obstruction. The resulting determinant-one comparison extends smoothly through each branch core by its first-order parallel gauge equation and the fixed isotropy model. Thus there is precisely one critical orbit for the actual determinant-one gauge group, not four artificial lift orbits. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 **Its actual Hessian is nondegenerate.** The adjoint local system decomposes on the product torus into the three real axes. Its two monodromy signs on these axes are $(1,-1)$, $(-1,1)$ and $(-1,-1)$. For a one-dimensional character $(u,v)$ the cellular torus complex is $\mathbb R\xleftarrow{\partial_1}\mathbb R^2\xleftarrow{\partial_2}\mathbb R$, with $\partial_1(x,y)=(u-1)x+(v-1)y$ and $\partial_2(z)=((1-v)z,(u-1)z)$. If $u-1\ne0$, the first map is onto, the second is injective, and its image is the kernel of the first by solving for $x$ in terms of $y$. If $v-1\ne0$, interchange the coordinates. This complex computes the flat first deformation classes directly: integrate a covariantly closed one-form on the simply connected rectangle to a primitive; its two edge period constants are $(x,y)$, equality around the square is $(1-v)x+(u-1)y=0$, and changing its initial primitive adds $((u-1)c,(v-1)c)$. This cochain complex is exact in degree one by solving with either nonzero coefficient, just as for the displayed chain complex. Integrating first in the product-interval direction reduces the exterior to that rectangle calculation. All three characters are therefore acyclic, in particular $H^1(T^2\times[s_0,s_1];\operatorname{ad})=0$. Any invariant infinitesimal flat deformation on the full orbifold is exact on this exterior. Its primitive extends through the branch cores: on the lifted normal disk its covariant derivative is the smooth deformation, so radial integration and the metric connection bound give a unique continuous limit; the same equation then bootstraps it smoothly, and equivariance passes to the limit. Thus the full invariant first deformation space is zero. Its zero space also vanishes by [F1]'s central stabilizer result. The compact selfadjoint gauge-fixed critical Hessian consequently has no kernel and is invertible. This proves nondegeneracy, rather than inferring it from the uniqueness of the critical orbit. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 **The rank-one complex and its differential.** Apply [F2]'s small all-index trajectory perturbation, keeping this unique critical point and its Hessian fixed. The complex has one rank-one integral orientation module. Every relative trajectory now starts and ends at that same critical point, so its relative class is a quotient loop and its index belongs to $4\mathbb Z$ by [F2]. There are no index-one trajectories. Thus its integral differential is zero. The chosen-data homology is $\mathbb Z$, and the independence theorem of [F2] identifies the group for any other regular choices. Tensoring this free group with $\mathbb Q$ gives dimension one. Changing its orientation basis reverses its generator; nothing in this computation singles out one sign. No claim about the held sutured closure or its point/surface eigenspaces was used. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth unknot and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smoothly embedded sphere transverse to $K$ in exactly two points. Write $B_1,B_2$ for its closed ball sides and $a_i=K\cap B_i$. For each $i$ there is an embedded disk $E_i\subset B_i$ with boundary $a_i\cup b_i$, where $b_i\subset S$ is a simple arc with the same endpoints as $a_i$, and $\operatorname{int}E_i\subset\operatorname{int}B_i$. Thus both ball arcs are boundary-parallel. Disks and arcs may have the usual rounded corners at the two endpoints.

## Statement references

[[def-countable-choice]]

[[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]]

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable choice, the smooth unknot and the transverse two-point sphere.

[F1] An unknot is ambient isotopic to the standard round circle; carrying its planar spanning disk through that isotopy gives a smooth embedded spanning disk. ([[def-knot-connected-sum-and-prime-knot]])

[F2] A compact embedded surface whose boundary is transverse to a closed embedded surface can be made transverse by an isotopy fixed near its boundary, under countable choice. ([[lem-relative-transversality-for-embedded-surfaces]], [[def-countable-choice]])

[F3] The two closed sides of a smooth embedded sphere in $S^3$ are smooth balls under countable choice. ([[thm-smooth-schoenflies-for-embedded-two-sphere-in-s-three]])

[F4] A regular nullhomotopic circle in a surface bounds a disk region; on a sphere there are two complementary disk regions. For a circle on the given sphere, [F3] identifies the sphere with the standard sphere, and stereographic projection from a point outside the circle supplies a planar linear nullhomotopy. The finite surface normal forms also show that a proper embedded arc in a disk splits it into two disks. For smooth input these disk regions inherit smooth interiors and can have corners rounded in boundary coordinates. ([[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]])

## Proof

1.1 Take a smooth spanning disk $E$ for $K$ from [F1] and make it transverse to $S$ using [F2]. Its intersection with $S$ is a compact one-manifold with boundary exactly the two points $K\cap S$. Consequently it consists of one proper arc $\alpha\subset E$ and finitely many circles. Indeed every compact one-manifold has finitely many interval and circle components, and precisely one interval is needed to account for these two boundary points. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 If circles occur, choose a circle $c$ bounding a disk $Q\subset S$ whose interior contains neither $\alpha$ nor another intersection circle. Such a choice exists by finite nesting. The disjoint circles cut the sphere into regions with a tree as dual graph: each additional separating circle splits one region in two. Root this tree at the region containing the connected arc $\alpha$ and take a leaf other than the root. Its closure is the required disk $Q$, using the sphere disk regions in [F4]. Thus $\operatorname{int}Q\cap E=\varnothing$ and $Q\cap K=\varnothing$. The circle $c$ also bounds a subdisk $E_c$ in the interior of $E$. This subdisk misses $\alpha$, since $\alpha$ is connected, disjoint from $c$ and has its endpoints on $\partial E$. [F4, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Replace $E_c$ by a nearby parallel copy of $Q$, keeping the component with the original boundary $K$. This yields another embedded spanning disk. To see this locally, the interior of $Q$ misses $E$ by step 2.1; push it a sufficiently small distance to the side of $S$ containing the retained collar of $E\setminus E_c$, and join it to that collar in product coordinates along $c$. The push and corner rounding introduce no intersection with $S$ or with the retained disk. Outside this collar everything is unchanged. The operation removes $c$ and any intersection circles in $E_c$, introduces none, and preserves $\alpha$. Repeating finitely often produces an embedded spanning disk, still denoted $E$, with $E\cap S=\alpha$. No assertion that these disk replacements are ambient isotopies is needed. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Cut this disk along $\alpha$. By [F4] there are two disks, each bounded by $\alpha$ and one of the two arcs into which $K\cap S$ divides $K$. Their interiors miss $S$. Near $\alpha$, transversality places the two disk interiors on opposite sides of $S$; connectedness keeps each interior on its respective side. By [F3] these are the two balls $B_1,B_2$, and the corresponding boundary arcs of $K$ are $a_1,a_2$. The two cut disks are therefore the required $E_i$, with $b_i=\alpha$ on their common boundary sphere. Local endpoint coordinates provide the stated corner convention. [F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎
